nodes.name: Radon-Nikodym property (RNP)
nodes.statement: A Banach space $V$ has the \emph{Radon-Nikod\'ym property} (RNP) if every Lipschitz map from $\mathbb{R} \to V$ is differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere.
differentia: every Lipschitz map from $\mathbb{R} \to V$ is differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere

nodes.name: RNP space
nodes.statement: We also say that $V$ is an \emph{RNP space}.

nodes.name: Local-to-global biLipschitz embeddability into RNP spaces
nodes.statement: If a complete metric space locally biLipschitz embeds into RNP spaces, must the entire space?
nodes.label: q:localembed

nodes.name: Compact-to-global biLipschitz embeddability into RNP spaces
nodes.statement: If every compact subset of a metric space biLipschitz embeds into an RNP space, must the entire space?
nodes.label: q:compactembed

nodes.name: BiLipschitz embeddability of complete discrete spaces into RNP spaces
nodes.statement: Does every complete, discrete metric space biLipschitz embed into an RNP space?
nodes.label: q:discreteembed

nodes.name: Uniformly discrete metric space
nodes.statement: A metric space $(X,d)$ is \emph{uniformly discrete} if there exists $\theta > 0$ such that $d(x,y) > \theta$ for all $x \neq y \in X$.
differentia: there exists $\theta > 0$ such that $d(x,y) > \theta$ for all $x \neq y \in X$

nodes.name: Kalton's theorem (uniformly discrete spaces)
nodes.statement: If $X$ is uniformly discrete, then $\LF{X}$ has the RNP.
nodes.label: thm:unifdiscrete

nodes.name: Pointed metric space (basepoint)
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space with distinguished basepoint $0 \in X$.

nodes.name: Lipschitz space Lip_0(X)
nodes.statement: Let $\Lip{X}$ denote the Banach space of Lipschitz functions $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $f(0)= 0$ equipped with the norm $\|f\| := \sup_{p \neq q} \frac{|f(p)-f(q)|}{d(p,q)}$.
nodes.genus: the Banach space of Lipschitz functions $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$
nodes.statement_short: Lip_0(X): Lipschitz functions vanishing at the basepoint, normed by the Lipschitz constant.

nodes.name: Dirac evaluation functionals delta_p
nodes.statement: The space $X$ isometrically embeds into $\Lip{X}^*$ via $p \mapsto \delta_p$, where $\delta_p(f) = f(p)$.

nodes.name: LF_fin(X) and LF(X)
nodes.statement: The linear span of $\{\delta_p\}_{p \in X}$ in $\Lip{X}^*$ is denoted by $\LFf{X}$, and its closure by $\LF{X}$.

nodes.name: Lipschitz free space
nodes.statement: The space $\LF{X}$ is called the \emph{Lipschitz free space over $X$}.

nodes.name: n-discrete metric space
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. For $r > 0$ and $p \in X$, $\boldsymbol{B_r(p)} := \{x \in X: d(x,p) \leq r\}$. We define the class of $\boldsymbol{n}$\textbf{-discrete} metric spaces recursively. A metric space is $0$-discrete if it is finite. A metric space $X$ is $(n+1)$-discrete if there exists $\theta > 0$ such that $B_\theta(p)$ is $n$-discrete for all $p \in X$.
nodes.statement_short: Closed balls $B_r(p)$; recursively, 0-discrete = finite, (n+1)-discrete = some radius $\theta$ gives n-discrete balls everywhere.

nodes.name: n-discrete spaces are discrete and complete
nodes.statement: Every $n$-discrete metric space is discrete and complete.

nodes.name: Uniformly discrete spaces are 1-discrete
nodes.statement: Uniformly discrete metric spaces are $1$-discrete.

nodes.name: Finite unions of n-discrete spaces
nodes.statement: The union of finitely many $n$-discrete metric spaces inside an ambient metric space is again $n$-discrete.
assumptions: finitely many $n$-discrete metric spaces inside an ambient metric space

nodes.name: n-discrete implies (n+1)-discrete, strictly
nodes.statement: Every $n$-discrete metric space is also $(n+1)$-discrete, but not conversely.

nodes.name: Construction of (n+1)-discrete spaces that are not n-discrete
nodes.statement: Here is a way to construct $(n+1)$-discrete metric spaces that are not $n$-discrete: Obviously, there are $1$-discrete metric spaces that are not $0$-discrete (for example, any infinite uniformly discrete space). Now take any metric space $(X,d)$ with $\diam{X} = 1$ that is $n$-discrete but not $(n-1)$-discrete. Let $Y$ be the disjoint union of the spaces $\{(X,\frac{1}{k}d)\}_{k=1}^\infty$, where the distance between any two points in different copies of $X$ is 1. Then $Y$ is $(n+1)$-discrete but not $n$-discrete.
nodes.statement_short: Construction: scaled disjoint copies $(X,\frac1k d)$ of an n- but not (n-1)-discrete space give an (n+1)- but not n-discrete space.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: Here is a way to construct $(n+1)$-discrete metric spaces that are not $n$-discrete: Obviously, there are $1$-discrete metric spaces that are not $0$-discrete (for example, any infinite uniformly discrete space).
nodes.statement_short: 1-discrete but not 0-discrete examples exist.

nodes.name: Scaled disjoint union
nodes.statement: Now take any metric space $(X,d)$ with $\diam{X} = 1$ that is $n$-discrete but not $(n-1)$-discrete. Let $Y$ be the disjoint union of the spaces $\{(X,\frac{1}{k}d)\}_{k=1}^\infty$, where the distance between any two points in different copies of $X$ is 1.
nodes.statement_short: Take X n- not (n-1)-discrete with diameter 1 and form Y from scaled copies.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Then $Y$ is $(n+1)$-discrete but not $n$-discrete.
nodes.statement_short: Y is (n+1)- but not n-discrete.

nodes.name: Local-to-global RNP for Lipschitz free spaces
nodes.statement: If $X$ is complete and locally compact and $\LF{K}$ has the RNP for every $K \subseteq X$ compact, must $\LF{X}$ have the RNP?

nodes.name: Schur property and approximation property
nodes.statement: Recall that a Banach space has the \emph{Schur property} if every weakly null sequence is norm null, and the \emph{approximation property} (AP) if every bounded operator on the space is the limit of a net of finite rank operators with respect to the topology of uniform convergence on compacta (henceforth, ucc).
nodes.statement_short: Schur: weakly null sequences are norm null; AP: every bounded operator is a ucc-limit of finite rank operators.

nodes.name: Ideal of closed sets; locally-I
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a metric space. Let $\boldsymbol{\Cl{X}}$ denote the set of closed subsets of $X$. A collection $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ is called an \textbf{ideal} if \begin{itemize} \item $\emptyset \in \mathcal{I}$, \item $\Cl{X} \ni A \subseteq B \in \mathcal{I}$ implies $A \in \mathcal{I}$, \item $A,B \in \mathcal{I}$ implies $A \cup B \in \mathcal{I}$. \end{itemize} When $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ is an ideal, a closed subset $E \subseteq X$ is said to be \textbf{locally modeled on} $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{I}}$, or just \textbf{locally-}$\boldsymbol{\mathcal{I}}$, if for every $p \in E$, there exists a radius $\theta > 0$ (depending on $p$) such that $E \cap B_\theta(p) \in \mathcal{I}$.
nodes.statement_short: Ideal: family of closed sets containing $\emptyset$, closed under closed subsets and finite unions; E is locally-I if each point has a ball whose trace on E lies in I.

nodes.name: Schur property over locally countable locally compact spaces
nodes.statement: The Lipschitz free space over every complete, locally countable, locally compact metric space has the Schur property.
assumptions: complete, locally countable, locally compact metric space

nodes.name: Proof of Schur corollary
nodes.statement: This follows from Theorem \ref{thm:Schur}, \cite[Theorem 3.1]{LancienSchur}, and the fact that the countable, compact subsets of a metric space form an ideal. The theorem \cite[Theorem 3.1]{LancienSchur} states that the Lipschitz free space over every countable compact metric space has the Schur property.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 1 (Schur) with the ideal of countable compact sets and Lancien et al.'s theorem.

nodes.name: Schur property for countable compact spaces
nodes.statement: The theorem \cite[Theorem 3.1]{LancienSchur} states that the Lipschitz free space over every countable compact metric space has the Schur property.
conclusions: the Lipschitz free space over every countable compact metric space has the Schur property

nodes.name: Doubling metric space
nodes.statement: Recall that a metric space $X$ is \emph{doubling} if there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $r > 0$ and $p \in X$, there exists $\{p_i\}_{i=1}^N \subseteq X$ such that $B_r(p) \subseteq \cup_{i=1}^N B_{r/2}(p_i)$.
differentia: there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $r > 0$ and $p \in X$, there exists $\{p_i\}_{i=1}^N \subseteq X$ such that $B_r(p) \subseteq \cup_{i=1}^N B_{r/2}(p_i)$

nodes.name: AP over locally countable compact or locally doubling spaces
nodes.statement: The Lipschitz free space over every complete metric space that is locally countable and locally compact or locally doubling has the AP (in particular, this holds for every connected complete Riemannian manifold).
assumptions: complete metric space that is locally countable and locally compact or locally doubling

nodes.name: Proof of AP corollary
nodes.statement: This follows from Theorem \ref{thm:AP}, \cite[Theorem 3.1]{Daletcompact}, \cite[Corollary 2.2]{Lanciendoubling}, and the fact that countable, compact, and doubling subsets of a metric space form ideals. The theorem \cite[Theorem 3.1]{Daletcompact} implies that the Lipschitz free space over a countable, compact metric space has the AP, and \cite[Corollary 2.2]{Lanciendoubling} implies that the Lipschitz free space over a doubling metric space has the AP.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem (AP) with the ideals of countable compact and doubling sets, using Dalet and Lancien-Pernecka.

nodes.name: AP for countable compact and doubling spaces
nodes.statement: The theorem \cite[Theorem 3.1]{Daletcompact} implies that the Lipschitz free space over a countable, compact metric space has the AP, and \cite[Corollary 2.2]{Lanciendoubling} implies that the Lipschitz free space over a doubling metric space has the AP.
conclusions: the Lipschitz free space over a countable, compact metric space has the AP
the Lipschitz free space over a doubling metric space has the AP

nodes.name: Known metric spaces with RNP free spaces
nodes.statement: We conclude the introduction by recording additional metric spaces whose Lipschitz free space is known to have the RNP. \begin{itemize} \item Spaces that biLipschitz embed into a proper metric space distorted by a nontrivial gauge or into a separable dual Banach space distorted by a nontrivial gauge (\cite[Proposition 6.3]{K}). \item Proper countable spaces (\cite[Theorem 2.1]{Daletproper}). \item Spaces that biLipschitz embed into an ultrametric space (\cite[Theorem 2]{Cuth}). \item Separable, complete metric spaces with null Hausdorff-1 measure that biLipschitz embed into $\mathbb{R}$-trees (\cite[Theorem 1.2]{APP1}).
nodes.statement_short: List of previously known classes of metric spaces whose Lipschitz free space has the RNP.

nodes.name: Comparison with Aliaga-Petitjean-Prochazka
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{thm:Schur} implies that $\LF{X}$ has the Schur property whenever $X$ is complete and locally compact and $\LF{K}$ has the Schur property for every $K \subseteq X$ compact, and \cite[Corollary 2.6]{APP2} implies the same conclusion assuming only that $X$ is complete and not locally compact.
nodes.statement_short: The Schur theorem covers locally compact X; [APP2] obtains the same without local compactness.

nodes.name: Duality LF(X)* = Lip_0(X)
nodes.statement: The first fundamental fact is that $\LF{X}^* = \Lip{X}$ (\cite[Theorem 2.2.2]{W}) and that, on bounded sets, the weak* topology is the topology of pointwise convergence.
conclusions: on bounded sets, the weak* topology is the topology of pointwise convergence

nodes.name: Off-diagonal set X tilde
nodes.statement: Let $\Delta \subseteq X \times X$ denote the diagonal and set $\tilde{X} := X \times X \setminus \Delta$.

nodes.name: Weighted l1 space l^1(X tilde)/d
nodes.statement: Let $\ell^1(\tilde{X})/d$ denote the Banach space of functions $b: \tilde{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ equipped with the norm $\|b\| := \sum_{(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q)$.

nodes.name: Quotient map from l^1(X tilde)/d onto LF(X)
nodes.statement: The second fundamental fact is that there is a linear quotient map $\pi: \ell^1(\tilde{X})/d \to \LF{X}$ defined by $\pi(b) = \sum_{(p,q)}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q)$.
conclusions: there is a linear quotient map $\pi: \ell^1(\tilde{X})/d \to \LF{X}$ defined by $\pi(b) = \sum_{(p,q)}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q)$

nodes.name: Isometric embedding of LF(Y) into LF(X)
nodes.statement: The third fundamental fact is that if $0 \in Y \subseteq X$, the natural inclusion $\LF{Y} \hookrightarrow \LF{X}$ is an isometric embedding.
conclusions: the natural inclusion $\LF{Y} \hookrightarrow \LF{X}$ is an isometric embedding

nodes.name: McShane extension theorem
nodes.statement: This is due to the \emph{McShane extension theorem}: every Lipschitz function from $Y$ to $\mathbb{R}$ can be extended to a Lipschitz function on all of $X$ without increasing the Lipschitz norm (\cite[Theorem 1.5.6(a)]{W}).
conclusions: every Lipschitz function from $Y$ to $\mathbb{R}$ can be extended to a Lipschitz function on all of $X$ without increasing the Lipschitz norm

nodes.name: Support of a Lipschitz function
nodes.statement: For $f \in \Lip{X}$, we define $\boldsymbol{\supp{f}} := \overline{f^{-1}(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\})}$.

nodes.name: Support of a finitely supported element
nodes.statement: For $v \in \LFf{X}$, we define $\boldsymbol{\supp{v}} := \bigcap \{E \subseteq X: v \in \text{span}\{\delta_p\}_{p \in E}\}$.

nodes.name: Functionals depend only on values on the support
nodes.statement: An obvious but important observation is that if $f$ and $g$ agree on $\supp{v}$, then $v(f) = v(g)$.

nodes.name: Kalton's reduction to bounded subsets
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a metric space and let $P$ be either the Schur, Radon-Nikod\'ym, or approximation property. If $\LF{Y}$ has $P$ for all $Y \subseteq X$ closed and bounded, then $\LF{X}$ has $P$.
assumptions: $P$ be either the Schur, Radon-Nikod\'ym, or approximation property
$\LF{Y}$ has $P$ for all $Y \subseteq X$ closed and bounded
nodes.label: thm:Kalton

nodes.name: Diameter
nodes.statement: The diameter of $X$ is defined by $\boldsymbol{\diam{X}} := \sup_{x,y \in X} d(x,y)$.

nodes.name: Basepoint convention for diameter-1 spaces
nodes.statement: Whenever $\diam{X} = 1$, we assume it is equipped with basepoint $0 \in X$ satisfying $d(0,p) = 1$ for all $p \in X$.

nodes.name: Sup norm bounded by Lipschitz norm
nodes.statement: Note that this implies, for any $f \in \Lip{X}$, $\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{p \neq 0} \frac{|f(p)-f(0)|}{d(0,p)} \leq \|f\|$, and also, for any $p \in X \setminus \{0\}$, $\|\delta_p\| = 1$.

nodes.name: Ignoring the basepoint condition
nodes.statement: When constructing Lipschitz functions in $\Lip{X}$, we routinely ignore the requirement that $f$ vanishes at the basepoint. This is because the requirement can easily be met by subtracting a constant from the function, and this will never affect any of the other desired properties of our construction.

nodes.name: Neighbourhood B_r(E)
nodes.statement: For $r > 0$ and $E \subseteq X$, define $\boldsymbol{B_r(E)} = \cup_{p \in E} B_r(p)$.

nodes.name: Uniformly locally modeled sets; ulm-closure
nodes.statement: A collection $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ of closed subsets is \textbf{downward-closed} if $\emptyset \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\Cl{X} \ni A \subseteq B \in \mathcal{D}$ implies $A \in \mathcal{D}$. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a downward-closed collection. A set $E \in \Cl{D}$ is \textbf{uniformly locally modeled on} $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}$, or just \textbf{uniformly locally-}$\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}$, if there exists $\theta > 0$ (dependent on $E$, independent of $F$) such that for all finite $F \subseteq X$, $E \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{D}$. The collection of all such $E \in \Cl{X}$ is denoted \textbf{ulm}$\boldsymbol{(\mathcal{D})}$. The downward-closed condition implies $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \ulm{\mathcal{D}}$ and that $\ulm{\mathcal{D}}$ is also downward-closed. Also, whenever $\mathcal{I}$ is an ideal, $\ulm{\mathcal{I}}$ is an ideal. A downward-closed collection $\mathcal{D}'$ is \textbf{ulm-closed} if $\ulm{\mathcal{D}'} = \mathcal{D}'$. The \textbf{ulm-closure} of a downward-closed collection $\mathcal{D}$, denoted $\boldsymbol{\ulmc{\mathcal{D}}}$, is the intersection of all downward-closed, ulm-closed collections containing $\mathcal{D}$. It is easy to verify that $\ulmc{\mathcal{D}}$ is always itself downward-closed and ulm-closed.
nodes.statement_short: ulm(D): closed sets whose intersections with $\theta$-neighbourhoods of finite sets lie in D for a uniform $\theta$; ulm-closure is the least ulm-closed downward-closed family containing D.
nodes.label: def:ulm

nodes.name: ulm-closure of an ideal is an ideal
nodes.statement: For all ideals $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$, $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ is an ideal.
nodes.label: prop:ulmcideal

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal. The subset $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ is downward-closed by definition, so we only need to show closure under finite unions. Set $\mathcal{B} := \{B \in \Cl{X}: \forall A \in \mathcal{I}, A \cup B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}\}$. Obviously $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathcal{B}$, and we'll show that $\mathcal{B}$ is ulm-closed. Let $B \in \ulm{\mathcal{B}}$. Let $\theta > 0$ such that $B \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{B}$ for all $F \subseteq X$ finite. Let $A \in \mathcal{I}$. Then for all $F \subseteq X$ finite, $(A \cup B) \cap B_\theta(F) = (A \cap B_\theta(F)) \cup (B \cap B_\theta(F)) \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ by definition of $\mathcal{B}$. Since $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ is ulm-closed, this shows $A \cup B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$. Since $A \in \mathcal{I}$ was arbitrary, this shows $B \in \mathcal{B}$ and thus $\mathcal{B} = \ulm{\mathcal{B}}$. We can conclude that whenever $A \in \mathcal{I}$ and $B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$, $A \cup B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$. Then we can consider the set $\mathcal{B}' := \{B \in \Cl{X}: \forall A \in \ulmc{I}, A \cup B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}\}$, so that the last sentence implies $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathcal{B}'$. By repeating the same argument, we get that $\mathcal{B}'$ is ulm-closed and thus $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}} \subseteq \mathcal{B}'$. By definition of $\mathcal{B}'$ this means $A \cup B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ whenever $A,B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show closure under unions in two rounds: the family of sets whose unions with I-sets stay in the closure is ulm-closed, then repeat with the closure.

nodes.name: Reduce to finite unions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal. The subset $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ is downward-closed by definition, so we only need to show closure under finite unions.
nodes.statement_short: Only closure under finite unions needs proof.

nodes.name: Auxiliary family B
nodes.statement: Set $\mathcal{B} := \{B \in \Cl{X}: \forall A \in \mathcal{I}, A \cup B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}\}$. Obviously $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathcal{B}$, and we'll show that $\mathcal{B}$ is ulm-closed.
nodes.statement_short: Define B; it contains I; aim to show B ulm-closed.

nodes.name: Take B in ulm(B)
nodes.statement: Let $B \in \ulm{\mathcal{B}}$. Let $\theta > 0$ such that $B \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{B}$ for all $F \subseteq X$ finite. Let $A \in \mathcal{I}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix B in ulm(B), its radius $\theta$, and A in I.

nodes.name: B is ulm-closed
nodes.statement: Then for all $F \subseteq X$ finite, $(A \cup B) \cap B_\theta(F) = (A \cap B_\theta(F)) \cup (B \cap B_\theta(F)) \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ by definition of $\mathcal{B}$. Since $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ is ulm-closed, this shows $A \cup B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$. Since $A \in \mathcal{I}$ was arbitrary, this shows $B \in \mathcal{B}$ and thus $\mathcal{B} = \ulm{\mathcal{B}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Unions localize, so A∪B lies in the closure; hence B = ulm(B).

nodes.name: First union property
nodes.statement: We can conclude that whenever $A \in \mathcal{I}$ and $B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$, $A \cup B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Unions of I-sets and closure sets stay in the closure.

nodes.name: Second round with B'
nodes.statement: Then we can consider the set $\mathcal{B}' := \{B \in \Cl{X}: \forall A \in \ulmc{I}, A \cup B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}\}$, so that the last sentence implies $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathcal{B}'$. By repeating the same argument, we get that $\mathcal{B}'$ is ulm-closed and thus $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}} \subseteq \mathcal{B}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the argument with B' to get ulmc(I) ⊆ B'.

nodes.name: Conclude closure under unions
nodes.statement: By definition of $\mathcal{B}'$ this means $A \cup B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ whenever $A,B \in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$.
nodes.statement_short: ulmc(I) is closed under unions.

nodes.name: ulm-closure equals locally-I sets
nodes.statement: For every ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$, $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ equals the collection of all locally-$\mathcal{I}$ subsets of $X$.
conclusions: $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ equals the collection of all locally-$\mathcal{I}$ subsets of $X$
nodes.statement_short: The ulm-closure of an ideal is exactly the family of locally-I closed sets.
nodes.label: thm:ulmclocallyI

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.3
nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Easy inclusion
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal. Let $\mathcal{D}$ denote the downward-closed collection of all locally-$\mathcal{I}$ closed subsets of $X$. Obviously $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ is ulm-closed, so we get $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Locally-I sets form an ulm-closed family containing I, so ulmc(I) ⊆ D.

nodes.name: Contrapositive reduction
nodes.statement: To prove the other containment, we prove that $\Cl{X} \setminus \ulmc{\mathcal{I}} \subseteq \Cl{X} \setminus \mathcal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show sets outside ulmc(I) are not locally-I.

nodes.name: Fix E and radii
nodes.statement: Let $E \in \Cl{X} \setminus \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$. Choose a sequence of radii $\theta_i \to 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Take E outside the closure and radii $\theta_i\to 0$.

nodes.name: First ball
nodes.statement: Then there is a finite subset $F \subseteq X$ such that $E \cap B_{\theta_1}(F) \not\in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$. Since $B_{\theta_1}(F) = \cup_{p \in F} B_{\theta_1}(p)$ and $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ is an ideal by Proposition \ref{prop:ulmcideal}, the previous sentence implies $E \cap B_{\theta_1}(p_1) \not\in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ for some $p_1 \in F$.
nodes.statement_short: Ideal property (Prop 3.2) gives a ball $B_{\theta_1}(p_1)$ with E∩ball outside the closure.

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: Repeating this argument again yields a point $p_2 \in X$ such that $E \cap B_{\theta_1}(p_1) \cap B_{\theta_2}(p_2) \not\in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$. Iterating, we can find a sequence of points $p_i \in X$ such that $\cap_{i=1}^N E \cap B_{\theta_i}(p_i) \not\in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ for all $N \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterating gives nested intersections outside the closure.

nodes.name: Limit point
nodes.statement: Let $p_i'$ be any sequence of points in $X$ with $p_N' \in \cap_{i=1}^N E \cap B_{\theta_i}(p_i)$. Since $\theta_i \to 0$, $E \in \Cl{X}$, and $X$ is complete, $p'_i \to p$ for some $p \in E$.
nodes.statement_short: Completeness gives a limit point p in E.

nodes.name: Every ball around p is bad
nodes.statement: For any $\theta > 0$, $E \cap B_\theta(p)$ contains $\cap_{i=1}^N E \cap B_{\theta_i}(p_i)$ for some sufficiently large $N$. Since $\ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$ is downward-closed and $\cap_{i=1}^N E \cap B_{\theta_i}(p_i) \not\in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$, this implies $E \cap B_\theta(p) \not\in \ulmc{\mathcal{I}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Downward closure gives E∩B_θ(p) ∉ ulmc(I).

nodes.name: E not locally-I
nodes.statement: In particular, $E \cap B_\theta(p) \not\in \mathcal{I}$. Hence $E \not\in \mathcal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence E is not in D.

nodes.name: Cut-off operator T*_{E,theta}
nodes.statement: Whenever $(X,d)$ is a bounded metric space with basepoint $0 \in X$, $E \subseteq X$, and $\theta > 0$, define the bounded operator $T^*_{E,\theta}: \Lip{X} \to \Lip{X}$ by $T^*_{E,\theta}(f)(x) = f(x)\cdot\max\{0,\min\{1,2-2\theta^{-1}d(E,x)\}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply f by a Lipschitz cut-off equal to 1 near E and 0 outside the $\theta$-neighbourhood of E.
nodes.label: def:T

nodes.name: Properties of the cut-off operators
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a metric space. Assume $\diam{X} = 1$. For any $E \subseteq X$ and $\theta > 0$, $T^*_{E,\theta}$ has a predual $T_{E,\theta}: \LF{X} \to \LF{X}$ and \begin{itemize} \item $\|T^*_{E,\theta}\|,\|T_{E,\theta}\|$ are bounded by a function of $\theta$, $C(\theta)$ (independent of $E$). \item For any $f \in \Lip{X}$ and $v \in \LFf{X}$, $\supp{T^*_{E,\theta}(f)} \subseteq \supp{f} \cap B_\theta(E)$ and $\supp{T_{E,\theta}(v)} \subseteq \supp{v} \cap B_\theta(E)$. \item For any $v \in \LFf{X}$, $\supp{v-T_{E,\theta}(v)} \subseteq \supp{v} \setminus B_{\theta/2}(E)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The cut-off operator has a predual T, both bounded by $C(\theta)$, and they localize supports to the $\theta$-neighbourhood of E.
nodes.label: prop:T

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.2
nodes.statement: That $T_{E,\theta}^*$ has a predual is due to the fact that it preserves pointwise convergence of functions. The boundedness of $T_{E,\theta}$ comes from the inequality $\|fg\| \leq \|f\|\|g\|_\infty + \|f\|_\infty\|g\| \leq 2\|f\|\|g\|$. The other statements are straightforward to check and we leave the details to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Weak*-continuity gives the predual; the Leibniz-type bound on $\|fg\|$ gives boundedness; the rest is routine.

nodes.name: Existence of predual
nodes.statement: That $T_{E,\theta}^*$ has a predual is due to the fact that it preserves pointwise convergence of functions.
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise-convergence preservation gives a predual.

nodes.name: Boundedness
nodes.statement: The boundedness of $T_{E,\theta}$ comes from the inequality $\|fg\| \leq \|f\|\|g\|_\infty + \|f\|_\infty\|g\| \leq 2\|f\|\|g\|$. The other statements are straightforward to check and we leave the details to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Product estimate gives the bound; other properties left to reader.

nodes.name: Local-to-global Schur property
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a complete metric space and $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ an ideal such that $X$ is locally-$\mathcal{I}$. If $\LF{A}$ has the Schur property for every $A \in \mathcal{I}$, then $\LF{X}$ has the Schur property.
assumptions: $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ an ideal such that $X$ is locally-$\mathcal{I}$
$\LF{A}$ has the Schur property for every $A \in \mathcal{I}$
also_stated_at: Let $X$ be a complete metric space and $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ an ideal such that $X$ is locally-$\mathcal{I}$. If $\LF{A}$ has the Schur property for every $A \in \mathcal{I}$, then $\LF{X}$ has the Schur property.
nodes.label: thm:Schur

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.3
nodes.statement: Assume $\LF{A}$ has the Schur property for all $A \in \mathcal{I}$. By Theorem \ref{thm:Kalton}, we may assume $X$ is bounded. By scaling the metric, we may assume $\diam{X} = 1$. Let $\mathcal{D}$ denote the downward-closed collection of all subsets $E \subseteq X$ such that $\LF{E}$ has the Schur property. By assumption, $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$. We will show $\mathcal{D}$ is ulm-closed, and thus $X \in \mathcal{D}$ by Theorem \ref{thm:ulmclocallyI} and the assumption that $X$ is locally-$\mathcal{I}$. Suppose $G \in \ulm{\mathcal{D}}$. Let $v_n \in \LF{G}$ such that $v_n$ is weakly null. It suffices to assume $v_n$ belongs to the dense subspace $\LFf{G} \subseteq \LF{G}$, and it suffices to find a norm null subsequence. Let $\theta > 0$ such that for all $F \subseteq X$ finite, $G \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{D}$. Set $N_1 := 1$ and $F_1 := \supp{v_1}$. By Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $T_{F_1,\theta}(v_n) \in \LF{G \cap B_\theta(F_1)}$. Thus, by definition of $\mathcal{D}$, $T_{F_1,\theta}(v_n)$ is norm null. Then we can find $N_2 > N_1$ large enough so that $\|T_{F_1,\theta}(v_{N_2})\| \leq 1$. Set $F_2 := F_1 \cup \supp{v_{N_2}}$. By Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $T_{F_2,\theta}(v_n) \in \LF{G \cap B_\theta(F_2)}$. Thus, by definition of $\mathcal{D}$, $T_{F_2,\theta}(v_n)$ is norm null. Then we can find $N_3 > N_2$ large enough so that $\|T_{F_2,\theta}(v_{N_3})\| \leq 1/2$, and we set $F_3 := F_2 \cup \supp{v_{N_3}}$. Continuing in this way, we can find an increasing sequence of finite subsets $F_1 \subseteq F_2 \subseteq \dots \subseteq X$ and numbers $N_1 < N_2 < \dots$ such that $\supp{v_{N_i}} \subseteq F_i$ and $\|T_{F_i,\theta}(v_{N_{i+1}})\| \leq 1/i$ for all $i \geq 1$. Then we form a new sequence $\tilde{v}_i$ defined by $\tilde{v}_1 := v_1$ and $\tilde{v}_{i+1} := v_{N_{i+1}} - T_{F_i,\theta}(v_{N_{i+1}})$ for $i \geq 1$. The sequence $\tilde{v}_i$ is norm-equivalent to a subsequence of $v_n$, so it suffices to prove that this sequence is norm null. By Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $d(\supp{\tilde{v}_{i}},\supp{\tilde{v}_{j}}) \geq \theta/2$ for all $i \neq j$. Let $f_i \in B_{\Lip{\supp{\tilde{v}_i}}}$ such that $\tilde{v}_i(f_i) = \|\tilde{v}_i\|$. Then we define $f(x) := f_i(x)$ if $x \in \supp{\tilde{v}_i}$, and note that the inequality $d(\supp{\tilde{v}_{i}},\supp{\tilde{v}_{j}}) \geq \theta/2$ and the assumption $\diam{X} = 1$ imply $\|f\| \leq \sup_i \{\|f_i\|,\frac{\|f_i\|_\infty+\|f_i\|_\infty}{\theta/2}\} \leq 4\theta^{-1}$. Thus, since $\tilde{v}_i$ is weakly null, we have $\|\tilde{v}_i\| = \tilde{v}_i(f) \to 0$. This proves that $\LF{G}$ has the Schur property. Hence, $G \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\ulm{\mathcal{D}} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the family of Schur subsets is ulm-closed: use cut-offs to build a subsequence with $\theta/2$-separated supports, then glue norming functions. Separation turns weak nullity into norm nullity.

nodes.name: Reduce to diameter 1
nodes.statement: Assume $\LF{A}$ has the Schur property for all $A \in \mathcal{I}$. By Theorem \ref{thm:Kalton}, we may assume $X$ is bounded. By scaling the metric, we may assume $\diam{X} = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: By Kalton's theorem and scaling assume diam X = 1.

nodes.name: Family D of Schur sets
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}$ denote the downward-closed collection of all subsets $E \subseteq X$ such that $\LF{E}$ has the Schur property. By assumption, $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$. We will show $\mathcal{D}$ is ulm-closed, and thus $X \in \mathcal{D}$ by Theorem \ref{thm:ulmclocallyI} and the assumption that $X$ is locally-$\mathcal{I}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define D; it contains I; showing D ulm-closed suffices by Theorem 3.3.

nodes.name: Fix G and weakly null sequence
nodes.statement: Suppose $G \in \ulm{\mathcal{D}}$. Let $v_n \in \LF{G}$ such that $v_n$ is weakly null. It suffices to assume $v_n$ belongs to the dense subspace $\LFf{G} \subseteq \LF{G}$, and it suffices to find a norm null subsequence.
nodes.statement_short: Take G in ulm(D) and finitely supported weakly null $v_n$; seek norm-null subsequence.

nodes.name: First cut-off
nodes.statement: Let $\theta > 0$ such that for all $F \subseteq X$ finite, $G \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{D}$. Set $N_1 := 1$ and $F_1 := \supp{v_1}$. By Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $T_{F_1,\theta}(v_n) \in \LF{G \cap B_\theta(F_1)}$. Thus, by definition of $\mathcal{D}$, $T_{F_1,\theta}(v_n)$ is norm null.
nodes.statement_short: Cut-off images lie in Schur pieces, hence are norm null; choose $N_2$.

nodes.name: Inductive choice of indices
nodes.statement: Then we can find $N_2 > N_1$ large enough so that $\|T_{F_1,\theta}(v_{N_2})\| \leq 1$. Set $F_2 := F_1 \cup \supp{v_{N_2}}$. By Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $T_{F_2,\theta}(v_n) \in \LF{G \cap B_\theta(F_2)}$. Thus, by definition of $\mathcal{D}$, $T_{F_2,\theta}(v_n)$ is norm null. Then we can find $N_3 > N_2$ large enough so that $\|T_{F_2,\theta}(v_{N_3})\| \leq 1/2$, and we set $F_3 := F_2 \cup \supp{v_{N_3}}$. Continuing in this way, we can find an increasing sequence of finite subsets $F_1 \subseteq F_2 \subseteq \dots \subseteq X$ and numbers $N_1 < N_2 < \dots$ such that $\supp{v_{N_i}} \subseteq F_i$ and $\|T_{F_i,\theta}(v_{N_{i+1}})\| \leq 1/i$ for all $i \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Iteratively choose $N_i$, $F_i$ with small cut-off parts.

nodes.name: Corrected sequence
nodes.statement: Then we form a new sequence $\tilde{v}_i$ defined by $\tilde{v}_1 := v_1$ and $\tilde{v}_{i+1} := v_{N_{i+1}} - T_{F_i,\theta}(v_{N_{i+1}})$ for $i \geq 1$. The sequence $\tilde{v}_i$ is norm-equivalent to a subsequence of $v_n$, so it suffices to prove that this sequence is norm null.
nodes.statement_short: Subtract cut-off parts to get $\tilde v_i$, equivalent to a subsequence.

nodes.name: Separated supports
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $d(\supp{\tilde{v}_{i}},\supp{\tilde{v}_{j}}) \geq \theta/2$ for all $i \neq j$.
nodes.statement_short: Supports of $\tilde v_i$ are $\theta/2$-separated.

nodes.name: Glue norming functions
nodes.statement: Let $f_i \in B_{\Lip{\supp{\tilde{v}_i}}}$ such that $\tilde{v}_i(f_i) = \|\tilde{v}_i\|$. Then we define $f(x) := f_i(x)$ if $x \in \supp{\tilde{v}_i}$, and note that the inequality $d(\supp{\tilde{v}_{i}},\supp{\tilde{v}_{j}}) \geq \theta/2$ and the assumption $\diam{X} = 1$ imply $\|f\| \leq \sup_i \{\|f_i\|,\frac{\|f_i\|_\infty+\|f_i\|_\infty}{\theta/2}\} \leq 4\theta^{-1}$. Thus, since $\tilde{v}_i$ is weakly null, we have $\|\tilde{v}_i\| = \tilde{v}_i(f) \to 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Glued function f has norm $\le 4/\theta$, so $\|\tilde v_i\| = \tilde v_i(f) \to 0$.

nodes.name: D is ulm-closed
nodes.statement: This proves that $\LF{G}$ has the Schur property. Hence, $G \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\ulm{\mathcal{D}} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: G in D, so ulm(D) ⊆ D.

nodes.name: Cut-off operators converge to identity
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a metric space. Assume $\diam{X} = 1$. For every $\theta > 0$, $T_{F,\theta}$ ucc-converges to Id$_{\LF{X}}$ as $F \to \infty$, $F$ finite.
nodes.label: prop:Tconv

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.1
nodes.statement: Since $\|T_{F,\theta}\|$ is uniformly bounded by a function of $\theta$ (independent of $F$), it suffices to check that $T_{F,\theta}$ pointwise converges to Id$_{\LF{X}}$ as $F \to \infty$ on a dense subset of $\LF{X}$. This happens on the dense subset $\LFf{X} \subseteq \LF{X}$ since whenever $v \in \LFf{X}$ and $F \supseteq \supp{v}$, $T_{F,\theta}(v) = v$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform boundedness reduces ucc-convergence to pointwise convergence on the dense finitely supported elements, where it is eventually exact.

nodes.name: Local-to-global approximation property
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a complete metric space and $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ an ideal such that $X$ is locally-$\mathcal{I}$. If, for every $A \in \mathcal{I}$, there exists $B \in \Cl{X}$ such that $A \subseteq B$ and $\LF{B}$ has the AP, then $\LF{X}$ has the AP.
assumptions: $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ an ideal such that $X$ is locally-$\mathcal{I}$
for every $A \in \mathcal{I}$, there exists $B \in \Cl{X}$ such that $A \subseteq B$ and $\LF{B}$ has the AP
also_stated_at: Let $X$ be a complete metric space and $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ an ideal such that $X$ is locally-$\mathcal{I}$. If, for every $A \in \mathcal{I}$, there exists $B \in \Cl{X}$ such that $A \subseteq B$ and $\LF{B}$ has the AP, then $\LF{X}$ has the AP.
nodes.label: thm:AP

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.2
nodes.statement: Assume that, for every $A \in \mathcal{I}$, there exists $B \in \Cl{X}$ such that $A \subseteq B$ and $\LF{B}$ has the AP. By Theorem \ref{thm:Kalton}, we may assume $X$ is bounded. By scaling the metric, we may assume $\diam{X} = 1$. Let $\mathcal{D}$ denote the downward-closed collection of all sets $E \subseteq X$ such that whenever $T \in \mathcal{B}(\LF{X},\LF{X})$ and $\mathrm{im}(T) \subseteq \LF{E}$, then $T$ belongs to the ucc-closure of the finite rank operators on $\LF{X}$. By assumption, $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$. We will show $\mathcal{D}$ is ulm-closed, and thus $X \in \mathcal{D}$ by Theorem \ref{thm:ulmclocallyI} and the assumption that $X$ is locally-$\mathcal{I}$. Suppose $G \in \ulm{\mathcal{D}}$. Let $T \in \mathcal{B}(\LF{X},\LF{X})$ such that $\mathrm{im}(T) \subseteq \LF{G}$. Let $\theta > 0$ such that for all $F \subseteq X$ finite, $G \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{D}$. By Proposition \ref{prop:T}, for each $F \subseteq X$ finite, $\mathrm{im}(T_{F,\theta} \circ T) \subseteq \LF{G \cap B_\theta(F)}$. By definition of $\mathcal{D}$, this implies each $T_{F,\theta} \circ T$ belongs to the ucc-closure of the finite rank operators on $\LF{X}$. By Proposition \ref{prop:Tconv}, the net of operators $T_{F,\theta} \circ T$ ucc-converges to $T$ as $F \to \infty$. This shows $T$ belongs to the ucc-closure of the finite rank operators on $\LF{X}$, and thus $G \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\ulm{\mathcal{D}} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the family of sets whose operators are ucc-approximable is ulm-closed, via the cut-off net $T_{F,\theta}\circ T \to T$.

nodes.name: Reduce to diameter 1
nodes.statement: Assume that, for every $A \in \mathcal{I}$, there exists $B \in \Cl{X}$ such that $A \subseteq B$ and $\LF{B}$ has the AP. By Theorem \ref{thm:Kalton}, we may assume $X$ is bounded. By scaling the metric, we may assume $\diam{X} = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: By Kalton's theorem and scaling assume diam X = 1.

nodes.name: Family D
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}$ denote the downward-closed collection of all sets $E \subseteq X$ such that whenever $T \in \mathcal{B}(\LF{X},\LF{X})$ and $\mathrm{im}(T) \subseteq \LF{E}$, then $T$ belongs to the ucc-closure of the finite rank operators on $\LF{X}$. By assumption, $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$. We will show $\mathcal{D}$ is ulm-closed, and thus $X \in \mathcal{D}$ by Theorem \ref{thm:ulmclocallyI} and the assumption that $X$ is locally-$\mathcal{I}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define D of sets whose operators are approximable; suffices D ulm-closed.

nodes.name: Fix G, T, theta
nodes.statement: Suppose $G \in \ulm{\mathcal{D}}$. Let $T \in \mathcal{B}(\LF{X},\LF{X})$ such that $\mathrm{im}(T) \subseteq \LF{G}$. Let $\theta > 0$ such that for all $F \subseteq X$ finite, $G \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take G in ulm(D), operator T into LF(G), and radius $\theta$.

nodes.name: Cut-off compositions approximable
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:T}, for each $F \subseteq X$ finite, $\mathrm{im}(T_{F,\theta} \circ T) \subseteq \LF{G \cap B_\theta(F)}$. By definition of $\mathcal{D}$, this implies each $T_{F,\theta} \circ T$ belongs to the ucc-closure of the finite rank operators on $\LF{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each $T_{F,\theta}\circ T$ maps into a set of D, hence is approximable.

nodes.name: Net converges to T
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:Tconv}, the net of operators $T_{F,\theta} \circ T$ ucc-converges to $T$ as $F \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: The net $T_{F,\theta}\circ T$ ucc-converges to T.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This shows $T$ belongs to the ucc-closure of the finite rank operators on $\LF{X}$, and thus $G \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\ulm{\mathcal{D}} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: T approximable, so G in D.

nodes.name: K-semi-embedding
nodes.statement: Let $K \in [1,\infty)$. A bounded linear map $T: V \to W$ between Banach spaces is a $\boldsymbol{K}$\textbf{-semi-embedding} if it is injective and $\overline{T(B_V)} \subseteq T(KB_V)$, where $B_V$ denotes the closed unit ball of $V$.
nodes.genus: A bounded linear map $T: V \to W$ between Banach spaces

nodes.name: Semi-embeddings preserve RNP
nodes.statement: A separable Banach space that $K$-semi-embeds into an RNP space has the RNP.
assumptions: A separable Banach space that $K$-semi-embeds into an RNP space
nodes.label: thm:semiembeddingRNP

nodes.name: Extension of semi-embedding result to general K
nodes.statement: The theorem is actually stated and proved only for $K=1$ in \cite{P}, but easily adapts to general $K$.

nodes.name: Standing assumption: diameter 1 with basepoint at distance 1
nodes.statement: For the remainder of the article, \textbf{fix a metric space} $\boldsymbol{(X,d)}$ with $\boldsymbol{\diam{X} = 1}$ and \textbf{basepoint} $\boldsymbol{0 \in X}$ with $\boldsymbol{d(0,p) = 1}$ for all $\boldsymbol{p \in X}$.

nodes.name: Spaces Lip_0(I,X) and LF(I,Y); restriction maps
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal. Let $\boldsymbol{\Lip{\mathcal{I},X}}$ denote the (not necessarily closed) subspace of $\Lip{X}$ consisting of functions $f$ with $\supp{f} \in \mathcal{I}$. We stress that the functions in $\Lip{\mathcal{I},X}$ are required to be globally defined on $X$ and not just on some set in $\mathcal{I}$. The subset $\Lip{\mathcal{I},X}$ is a subspace since $\mathcal{I}$ is an ideal. For each $p \in X$, we get a continuous linear functional $\delta_p \in \Lip{\mathcal{I},X}^*$ defined by $\delta_p(f) = f(p)$. For each subset $Y \subseteq X$, define $\boldsymbol{\LFf{\mathcal{I}}{Y}}$ to be the linear span of $\{\delta_p\}_{p \in Y}$ in $\Lip{\mathcal{I},X}^*$, and $\boldsymbol{\LF{\mathcal{I}}{Y}}$ its closure. We also stress that, despite the absence of `$X$' in the notation, the structure of the space $\LF{\mathcal{I}}{Y} \subseteq \Lip{\mathcal{I},X}^*$ depends not only on $Y$ but also $X$ because the functions in $\Lip{\mathcal{I},X}$ are required to be globally defined on $X$. If $v \in \LFf{\mathcal{I}}{X}$, we denote by $\supp{v}$ the smallest finite set $F$ such that $v \in$ span$\{\delta_p\}_{p \in F}$. We denote the norm on $\LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ by $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{I}}$. It of course holds that $\Lip{\Cl{X}}{X} = \Lip{X}$, $\LFf{\Cl{X}}{X} = \LFf{X}$, and $\LF{\Cl{X}}{X} = \LF{X}$. Whenever $\mathcal{I}_1 \supseteq \mathcal{I}_2$, we get a canonical restriction map $\boldsymbol{R^{\mathcal{I}_1}_{\mathcal{I}_2}}: \LFf{\mathcal{I}_1}{X} \to \LFf{\mathcal{I}_2}{X}$ which extends to a linear contraction $R^{\mathcal{I}_1}_{\mathcal{I}_2}: \LF{\mathcal{I}_1}{X} \to \LF{\mathcal{I}_2}{X}$. If $\mathcal{I}_1 = \Cl{X}$, we just write $R_{\mathcal{I}_2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lipschitz functions supported in sets of an ideal I; LF(I,Y) is the closed span of point evaluations in the dual; restriction maps between ideals.

nodes.name: Ideals Fin_n
nodes.statement: Define ideals $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{F}in_n} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ recursively, as follows: \begin{itemize} \item $\mathcal{F}in_0 := \boldsymbol{\mathcal{F}in} :=$ finite subsets of $X$. \item $\mathcal{F}in_{n+1} := \ulm{\mathcal{F}in_n}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Fin_0 = finite sets; Fin_{n+1} = ulm(Fin_n).

nodes.name: Fin_n consists of the n-discrete sets
nodes.statement: It holds that $Y \in \mathcal{F}in_n$ if and only if $Y$ is $n$-discrete.

nodes.name: RNP for LF(Fin_k, X)
nodes.statement: Assume $X$ is countable, $\diam{X} = 1$, and $X$ is $n$-discrete for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The space $\LF{\mathcal{F}in_k}{X}$ has the RNP for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$.
assumptions: $X$ is countable, $\diam{X} = 1$, and $X$ is $n$-discrete for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$
conclusions: The space $\LF{\mathcal{F}in_k}{X}$ has the RNP for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$
nodes.label: lem:RNP

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.5
nodes.statement: We will prove the theorem by induction. The base case is $k=0$, $\LF{\mathcal{F}in_0}{X} = \LF{\mathcal{F}in}{X}$. Corollary \ref{cor:predual} implies $\LF{\mathcal{F}in}{X}$ has the RNP since it is a separable dual. Now assume $\LF{\mathcal{F}in_k}{X}$ has the RNP for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Then since $\mathcal{F}in_{k+1} = \ulm{\mathcal{F}in_k}$, Theorem \ref{thm:semiembedding} and the inductive hypothesis imply $R^{\mathcal{F}in_{k+1}}_{\mathcal{F}in_k}: \LF{\mathcal{F}in_{k+1}}{X} \to \LF{\mathcal{F}in_k}{X}$ is a 7-semi-embedding from a separable space into an RNP space, hence $\LF{\mathcal{F}in_{k+1}}{X}$ has the RNP by Theorem \ref{thm:semiembeddingRNP}.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on k: base case is a separable dual; inductive step uses the 7-semi-embedding $R^{Fin_{k+1}}_{Fin_k}$ and Pisier's result.

nodes.name: Induction set-up
nodes.statement: We will prove the theorem by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on k.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: The base case is $k=0$, $\LF{\mathcal{F}in_0}{X} = \LF{\mathcal{F}in}{X}$. Corollary \ref{cor:predual} implies $\LF{\mathcal{F}in}{X}$ has the RNP since it is a separable dual.
nodes.statement_short: LF(Fin,X) is a separable dual, hence RNP.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Now assume $\LF{\mathcal{F}in_k}{X}$ has the RNP for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Then since $\mathcal{F}in_{k+1} = \ulm{\mathcal{F}in_k}$, Theorem \ref{thm:semiembedding} and the inductive hypothesis imply $R^{\mathcal{F}in_{k+1}}_{\mathcal{F}in_k}: \LF{\mathcal{F}in_{k+1}}{X} \to \LF{\mathcal{F}in_k}{X}$ is a 7-semi-embedding from a separable space into an RNP space, hence $\LF{\mathcal{F}in_{k+1}}{X}$ has the RNP by Theorem \ref{thm:semiembeddingRNP}.
nodes.statement_short: 7-semi-embedding into an RNP space transfers the RNP.

nodes.name: RNP for Lipschitz free spaces over n-discrete spaces
nodes.statement: For all $n$-discrete metric spaces $X$, $\LF{X}$ has the RNP.
also_stated_at: For all $n$-discrete metric spaces $X$, $\LF{X}$ has the RNP.
nodes.label: thm:RNP

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.6
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an $n$-discrete metric space. Theorem \ref{thm:Kalton} and the fact that $n$-discreteness passes to arbitrary subsets allows us to assume $X$ is bounded. By scaling, we may assume $\diam{X} = 1$. The RNP is separably determined (\cite[Corollary 2.12]{P}). Then since every separable subspace of $\LF{X}$ is contained in $\LF{Y}$ for some $Y \subseteq X$ countable, we may assume $X$ is countable. Then the conclusion follows from Lemma \ref{lem:RNP} and the fact that $\LF{X} = \LF{\Cl{X}}{X} = \LF{\mathcal{F}in_n}{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to bounded (Kalton), diameter 1, and countable X (RNP separably determined), then apply Lemma 6.5 with $LF(X) = LF(Fin_n,X)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to bounded, diameter 1
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an $n$-discrete metric space. Theorem \ref{thm:Kalton} and the fact that $n$-discreteness passes to arbitrary subsets allows us to assume $X$ is bounded. By scaling, we may assume $\diam{X} = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Kalton's theorem and scaling.

nodes.name: Reduce to countable X
nodes.statement: The RNP is separably determined (\cite[Corollary 2.12]{P}). Then since every separable subspace of $\LF{X}$ is contained in $\LF{Y}$ for some $Y \subseteq X$ countable, we may assume $X$ is countable.
nodes.statement_short: Separable determination of RNP.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 6.5
nodes.statement: Then the conclusion follows from Lemma \ref{lem:RNP} and the fact that $\LF{X} = \LF{\Cl{X}}{X} = \LF{\mathcal{F}in_n}{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude via Lemma 6.5 and LF(X) = LF(Fin_n,X).

nodes.name: Special case of the semi-embedding inequality
nodes.statement: For every ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ and $p,q_k \in X$, if \\ $R^{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\delta_p-\delta_{q_k}) \overset{k \to \infty}{\to} \delta_p$, then $\|\delta_p\|_{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}} \leq \liminf_{k \to \infty} \|\delta_p-\delta_{q_k}\|_{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}$.
nodes.label: prop:semiembeddingspecial

nodes.name: Radius rad_I(p)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal. For $p \in X$, we define $\boldsymbol{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}} := \sup \{r \leq \diam{X}: B_r(p) \in \mathcal{I}\}$, with the convention that $\sup \emptyset = 0$.

nodes.name: Norms of point masses via rad_I
nodes.statement: For all ideals $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ and $p,p' \in X$, $\|\delta_p\|_{\mathcal{I}} = \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ and $\|\delta_p-\delta_{p'}\|_{\mathcal{I}} = \min\{d(p,p'),\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: In LF(I,X), $\|\delta_p\| = rad_I(p)$ and $\|\delta_p-\delta_{p'}\| = \min\{d(p,p'), rad_I(p)+rad_I(p')\}$.
nodes.label: prop:radInorm

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.9
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I},p,p'$ be as above. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $f \in B_{\Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$. Then $\supp{f} \in \mathcal{I}$, so by definition of $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$, there exists $q \in B_{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\varepsilon}(p)$ such that $q \notin \supp{f}$. Hence, $d(p,q) \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\varepsilon$ and $f(q) = 0$. Since $\|f\| \leq 1$, it follows that $|\delta_p(f)| = |f(p)| \leq d(p,q) \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon > 0$ and $f \in B_{\Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$ were arbitrary, it follows that $\|\delta_p\|_{\mathcal{I}} \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. For the other inequality, it obviously suffices to assume $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} > 0$. Let $\varepsilon \in (0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p})$. Then define $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ by $f(x) = \max(0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon-d(p,x))$. Then $\|f\| \leq 1$ and $\supp{f} \subseteq B_{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon}(p) \in \mathcal{I}$. Thus, $\|\delta_p\|_{\mathcal{I}} \geq |\delta_p(f)| = f(p) = \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon \in (0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p})$ was arbitrary, we get $\|\delta_p\|_{\mathcal{I}} \geq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. This proves the first statement. For the second statement, we clearly have \\ $\|\delta_p-\delta_{p'}\|_{\mathcal{I}} \leq \min\{d(p,p'),\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}\}$. For the other inequality, there are three cases: \begin{enumerate} \item $d(p,p') \leq \max\{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}\}$, \item $\max\{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}\} \leq d(p,p') \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}$, \item $d(p,p') \geq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}$. \end{enumerate} In the first case, without loss of generality, assume $d(p,p') \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ and use the function $f(x) = \max(0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon-d(p,x))$. In the second case, define $f(x) = \max(0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon-d(p,x))$ and $g(x) = \max(0,d(p,p')-\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon-d(p',x))$ and use the function $f-g$. In the third case, $f(x) = \max(0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon-d(p,x))$ and $g(x) = \max(0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}-\varepsilon-d(p',x))$ and use the function $f-g$.
nodes.statement_short: Upper bounds via a zero of f near p; lower bounds via explicit tent functions, split into three cases for the two-point norm.

nodes.name: Fix data
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I},p,p'$ be as above. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $f \in B_{\Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\varepsilon$ and f in the unit ball.

nodes.name: Upper bound on norm of delta_p
nodes.statement: Then $\supp{f} \in \mathcal{I}$, so by definition of $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$, there exists $q \in B_{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\varepsilon}(p)$ such that $q \notin \supp{f}$. Hence, $d(p,q) \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\varepsilon$ and $f(q) = 0$. Since $\|f\| \leq 1$, it follows that $|\delta_p(f)| = |f(p)| \leq d(p,q) \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon > 0$ and $f \in B_{\Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$ were arbitrary, it follows that $\|\delta_p\|_{\mathcal{I}} \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. For the other inequality, it obviously suffices to assume $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: f vanishes near p, so $|f(p)| \le rad_I(p)+\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Lower bound via tent function
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon \in (0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p})$. Then define $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ by $f(x) = \max(0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon-d(p,x))$. Then $\|f\| \leq 1$ and $\supp{f} \subseteq B_{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon}(p) \in \mathcal{I}$. Thus, $\|\delta_p\|_{\mathcal{I}} \geq |\delta_p(f)| = f(p) = \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon \in (0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p})$ was arbitrary, we get $\|\delta_p\|_{\mathcal{I}} \geq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. This proves the first statement.
nodes.statement_short: A tent function supported in a ball in I gives the reverse inequality.

nodes.name: Second statement: three cases
nodes.statement: For the second statement, we clearly have \\ $\|\delta_p-\delta_{p'}\|_{\mathcal{I}} \leq \min\{d(p,p'),\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}\}$. For the other inequality, there are three cases: \begin{enumerate} \item $d(p,p') \leq \max\{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}\}$, \item $\max\{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}\} \leq d(p,p') \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}$, \item $d(p,p') \geq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound is clear; split lower bound into three cases.

nodes.name: Case 1
nodes.statement: In the first case, without loss of generality, assume $d(p,p') \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ and use the function $f(x) = \max(0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon-d(p,x))$.
nodes.statement_short: Use a single tent at p.

nodes.name: Case 2
nodes.statement: In the second case, define $f(x) = \max(0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon-d(p,x))$ and $g(x) = \max(0,d(p,p')-\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon-d(p',x))$ and use the function $f-g$.
nodes.statement_short: Use difference of truncated tents.

nodes.name: Case 3
nodes.statement: In the third case, $f(x) = \max(0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\varepsilon-d(p,x))$ and $g(x) = \max(0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p'}-\varepsilon-d(p',x))$ and use the function $f-g$.
nodes.statement_short: Use difference of two tents.

nodes.name: Uniform positivity of rad_I near ulm(I)-balls
nodes.statement: For all ideals $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$, $p \in X$, and \\ $r \in (0,\rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p})$, $\inf_{q \in B_r(p)} \rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} > 0$.
nodes.label: prop:radIinf

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.10
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I},p,r$ be as above. Choose $r' \in (r,\rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p})$. By definition of $\rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p}$, $B_{r'}(p) \in \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$. By definition of $\ulm{\mathcal{I}}$, there exists $\theta' > 0$ such that $B_{r'}(p) \cap B_{\theta'}(q) \in \mathcal{I}$ for every $q \in X$. Set $\theta := \min(\theta',r'-r)$. Then $B_\theta(q) \subseteq B_{r'}(p) \cap B_{\theta'}(q) \in \mathcal{I}$ for every $q \in B_r(p)$. Hence, by definition of $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$, $\inf_{q \in B_r(p)} \rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} \geq \theta > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Unwind the definitions of rad and ulm to find a uniform $\theta$ with $B_\theta(q)\in I$ for all q near p.

nodes.name: Choose r'
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I},p,r$ be as above. Choose $r' \in (r,\rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p})$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $r' \in (r, rad_{ulm(I)}(p))$.

nodes.name: Unwind definitions
nodes.statement: By definition of $\rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p}$, $B_{r'}(p) \in \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$. By definition of $\ulm{\mathcal{I}}$, there exists $\theta' > 0$ such that $B_{r'}(p) \cap B_{\theta'}(q) \in \mathcal{I}$ for every $q \in X$.
nodes.statement_short: Ball is in ulm(I), giving uniform $\theta'$.

nodes.name: Uniform radius
nodes.statement: Set $\theta := \min(\theta',r'-r)$. Then $B_\theta(q) \subseteq B_{r'}(p) \cap B_{\theta'}(q) \in \mathcal{I}$ for every $q \in B_r(p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Balls of radius $\theta$ around q in $B_r(p)$ lie in I.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, by definition of $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$, $\inf_{q \in B_r(p)} \rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} \geq \theta > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: inf of rad is at least $\theta$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.7
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal, $p,q_k \in X$, and assume $R^{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\delta_p-\delta_{q_k}) \overset{k \to \infty}{\to} \delta_p$. Then $\|\delta_{q_k}\|_{\mathcal{I}} \overset{k \to \infty}{\to} 0$. By Proposition \ref{prop:radInorm}, this is equivalent to $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_k} \overset{k \to \infty}{\to} 0$. Together with Proposition \ref{prop:radIinf}, this implies $\liminf_{k \to \infty} d(p,q_k) \geq \rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p}$. Thus, using Proposition \ref{prop:radInorm} again, $$\|\delta_p\|_{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}} = \rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p} \leq \liminf_{k \to \infty} \min\{d(p,q_k),\rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p}+\rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{q_k}\}$$ $$= \liminf_{k \to \infty}\|\delta_p-\delta_{q_k}\|_{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Convergence forces $rad_I(q_k)\to 0$, so by Prop 6.10 the $q_k$ stay away from p; then Prop 6.9 gives the norm inequality.

nodes.name: Hypothesis
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal, $p,q_k \in X$, and assume $R^{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\delta_p-\delta_{q_k}) \overset{k \to \infty}{\to} \delta_p$. Then $\|\delta_{q_k}\|_{\mathcal{I}} \overset{k \to \infty}{\to} 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Convergence gives $\|\delta_{q_k}\|_I \to 0$.

nodes.name: rad of q_k tends to 0
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:radInorm}, this is equivalent to $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_k} \overset{k \to \infty}{\to} 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate via Prop 6.9.

nodes.name: q_k stay far from p
nodes.statement: Together with Proposition \ref{prop:radIinf}, this implies $\liminf_{k \to \infty} d(p,q_k) \geq \rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p}$.
nodes.statement_short: Prop 6.10 gives liminf distance bound.

nodes.name: Norm inequality
nodes.statement: Thus, using Proposition \ref{prop:radInorm} again, $$\|\delta_p\|_{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}} = \rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p} \leq \liminf_{k \to \infty} \min\{d(p,q_k),\rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{p}+\rad{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{q_k}\}$$ $$= \liminf_{k \to \infty}\|\delta_p-\delta_{q_k}\|_{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Prop 6.9 again gives the claim.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 6.23
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem \ref{thm:semiembedding} in full is more complicated and requires a series of supporting lemmas and theorems. Figure \ref{fig:lemmas} shows the dependency structure. Theorem \ref{thm:quotient} is particularly important in understanding the structure of $\LF{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$. It generalizes Proposition \ref{prop:radInorm} and is used in different ways to understand both the domain of $R^{\mathcal{F}in_{n+1}}_{\mathcal{F}in_n}$ (through Lemma \ref{lem:quotientclose}) and its codomain (through Lemma \ref{lem:quotientfinite}). Consider a sequence $v_k \in B_{\LF{\mathcal{F}in_{n+1}}{X}}$ with $R^{\mathcal{F}in_{n+1}}_{\mathcal{F}in_n}(v_k) \overset{k \to \infty}{\to} u \in B_{\LF{\mathcal{F}in_{n}}{X}}$, as would be needed in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:semiembedding}. Set $r_p := (1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{F}in_{n+1}}{p}$. After throwing away a term from the image of $R_{\mathcal{F}in_n}$, Lemma \ref{lem:quotientfinite} lets us assume $u$ is finitely supported in each ball $B_{r_p}(p)$. After throwing away terms from the image of $R_{\mathcal{F}in_{n+1}}$, Lemma \ref{lem:quotientclose} allows us to assume $v_k = \tilde{a}_k + \sum_{i=1}^\infty v_k^i$, where $\tilde{a}_k$ comes from a dual space, $\sum_{i=1}^\infty \|v_k^i\|_{\mathcal{F}in_{n+1}} \leq 1$, and each $v_k^i$ is supported inside some ball $B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)$. Lemma \ref{lem:sequence2} is an important technical result that then lets us (eventually in $k$, depending on $i$) reduce the support of $v_k^i$ by intersecting it with the support of $u$. An essential input into the proof of this lemma is Lemma \ref{lem:isomorphism} (via Lemma \ref{lem:sequence1}), which allows us to ``upgrade" our mode of convergence from $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{F}in_n}$ to $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{F}in_{n+1}}$ inside the balls $B_{r_p}(p)$. Since each $v_k^i$ is supported in $B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)$ and $u$ is finitely supported in $B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)$, this means $v_k^i$ (eventually) belongs to a finite-dimensional space. Thus $v_k = \tilde{a}_k + \sum_{i=1}^\infty v_k^i$, and all the terms come from a dual space. By weak*-compactness, we get an ultralimit $v \in \LF{\mathcal{F}in_{n+1}}{X}$ that satisfies $R^{\mathcal{F}in_{n+1}}_{\mathcal{F}in_n}(v) = u$, as required.
nodes.section: 6.3 Proof Sketch of Theorem 6.23 and Outline of Lemma Structure
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: reduce u and $v_k$ to finitely supported pieces in small balls via Lemmas 6.17/6.18, upgrade convergence by Lemmas 6.15/6.21, then take a weak* ultralimit.
