nodes.name: Weighted space l^1_I(X) and map Q_I
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal. We define $\boldsymbol{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$ to be the Banach space of equivalence classes of real-valued functions $a: X \to \mathbb{R}$ with finite norm $\boldsymbol{\|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}} := \sum_{p \in X} |a_p|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. The equivalence relation is $a \sim b$ if $a_p = b_p$ for all $p \in X$ with $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} > 0$. We will abuse notation and continue to write $a$ for its equivalence class, but there should never be any trouble verifying well-definedness whenever it arises. Whenever $Y \subseteq X$, there is a closed subspace $\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y} = \{a \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}: \forall p \in X \setminus Y, a_p = 0\}$. Although `$X$' is absent from the notation, the structure of the space $\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ depends not only on $Y$ but also $X$ because $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ depends not only on $Y$ but also $X$, even if $p \in Y$. For $a \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$, we define $\supp{a} := \{p \in X: \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} > 0, a_p \neq 0\}$. By Proposition \ref{prop:radInorm}, the map $\boldsymbol{Q}_{\mathcal{I}}: \l{\mathcal{I}}{X} \to \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ defined by $Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a) = \sum_{p \in X} a_p\delta_p$ is a well-defined linear contraction.
nodes.statement_short: $\ell^1$ space weighted by $rad_I(p)$, its restrictions to subsets, supports, and the contraction $Q_I(a) = \sum a_p\delta_p$ into LF(I,X).

nodes.name: Quotient theorem for LF(I,Y)
nodes.statement: For all ideals $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ and subsets $Y \subseteq X$, $R_{\mathcal{I}} \oplus Q_{\mathcal{I}}: \LF{Y} \oplus_1 \l{\mathcal{I}}{Y} \to \LF{\mathcal{I},Y}$ is a quotient map; it maps the open ball onto the open ball.
conclusions: it maps the open ball onto the open ball
nodes.statement_short: LF(I,Y) is a quotient of $LF(Y) \oplus_1 \ell^1_I(Y)$ via $R_I \oplus Q_I$.
nodes.label: thm:quotient

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.12
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I},Y$ be as above. Let $v \in \LFf{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ with finite support $\supp{v} =: F \subseteq Y$ and $\|v\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$. We may assume $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} > 0$ for all $p \in F$ since otherwise $\delta_p = 0 \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$. Let $\ell^\infty_{\mathcal{I}}(F)$ denote the dual space (and predual) of $\l{\mathcal{I}}{F}$. Consider the map $T = (T_1,T_2): \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X} \to \Lip{F} \oplus_\infty \ell^\infty_{\mathcal{I}}(F)$ defined by $T_1(f) = f \big|_F$ and $T_2(f) = \sum_{p \in F} f(p)\mathsf{1}_p$. So both $T_1$ and $T_2$ are restriction maps of sorts. Set $V := \mathrm{im}(T)$. We claim that $T$ is a quotient onto $V$. Linearity is clear, and contractivity is as well as soon one recalls (from the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:radInorm}) that $|f(p)| \leq \|f\|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ whenever $f \in \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$. Now let $(f,\sum_{p \in F} f(p)\mathsf{1}_p) \in V$ with $\max_{p \in F} \{\|f\|,\frac{|f(p)|}{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}\} = 1-\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. In particular, $|f(p)| \leq (1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ for all $p \in F$. Extend the domain of $f$ to all of $X$ without increasing the Lipschitz norm using the McShane extension theorem, and call this extension $f'$. Define $F_+ := \{p \in F: f(p) > 0\}$ and $F_- := \{p \in F: f(p) < 0\}$. Define $g_+,g_-: X \to \mathbb{R}$ by $g_+(x) = \max_{p \in F_+} \{0,(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-d(p,x)\}$ and $g_-(x) = -\max_{p \in F_-} \{0,(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-d(p,x)\}$. Then $\|g_+\|,\|g_-\| \leq 1$, $g_+ \geq 0$, $g_- \leq 0$, and $\supp{g_+} \subseteq \cup_{p \in F_+} B_{(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}(p)$ and $\supp{g_-} \subseteq \cup_{p \in F_-} B_{(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}(p)$. Then $f'' := \max(g_-,\min(g_+,f'))$ satisfies $\|f''\| \leq 1$ and $\supp{f} \subseteq \cup_{p \in F} B_{(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}(p)$ which belongs to $\mathcal{I}$ since it is a finite union of sets which themselves belong to $\mathcal{I}$ by definition of $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. Also, the condition $|f(p)| \leq (1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ for all $p \in F$ implies $f''(p) = f(p)$ for all $p \in F$. This implies $T(f'') = (f,\sum_{p \in F} f(p)\mathsf{1}_p)$, proving that $T$ is a quotient map. $T^*: V^* \to \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}^*$ is then an isometric embedding. The image of $T^*$ is exactly the subspace of $\LFf{\mathcal{I}}{X} \subseteq \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}^*$ consisting of elements supported in $F$. In particular, $v \in \mathrm{im}(T^*)$. Since $V \subseteq \Lip{F} \oplus_\infty \ell^\infty_{\mathcal{I}}(F)$, there is a quotient map $S: \LF{F} \oplus_1 \l{\mathcal{I}}{F} \twoheadrightarrow V^*$ so that $T^* \circ S: \LF{F} \oplus_1 \l{\mathcal{I}}{F} \to \mathrm{im}(T^*)$ is a quotient map. Then since $v \in \mathrm{im}(T^*)$ with $\|v\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$, there are $w \in \LF{F} \subseteq \LF{Y}$ and $a \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{F} \subseteq \l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ such that $T^*(S(w,a)) = v$ and $\|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{F}} < 1$. It is easily seen that $T^*(S(w,a)) = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a)$, proving the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Dualize: the restriction map from Lip(I,X) to $Lip(F) \oplus_\infty \ell^\infty_I(F)$ is a quotient (McShane extension plus truncation by tents), so its adjoint is an isometric embedding.

nodes.name: Reduce to finitely supported v
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I},Y$ be as above. Let $v \in \LFf{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ with finite support $\supp{v} =: F \subseteq Y$ and $\|v\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$. We may assume $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} > 0$ for all $p \in F$ since otherwise $\delta_p = 0 \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take finitely supported v of norm <1 with positive radii on its support.

nodes.name: Restriction map T
nodes.statement: Let $\ell^\infty_{\mathcal{I}}(F)$ denote the dual space (and predual) of $\l{\mathcal{I}}{F}$. Consider the map $T = (T_1,T_2): \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X} \to \Lip{F} \oplus_\infty \ell^\infty_{\mathcal{I}}(F)$ defined by $T_1(f) = f \big|_F$ and $T_2(f) = \sum_{p \in F} f(p)\mathsf{1}_p$. So both $T_1$ and $T_2$ are restriction maps of sorts. Set $V := \mathrm{im}(T)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $T=(T_1,T_2)$ and its image V.

nodes.name: Claim: T is a quotient
nodes.statement: We claim that $T$ is a quotient onto $V$. Linearity is clear, and contractivity is as well as soon one recalls (from the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:radInorm}) that $|f(p)| \leq \|f\|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ whenever $f \in \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$. Now let $(f,\sum_{p \in F} f(p)\mathsf{1}_p) \in V$ with $\max_{p \in F} \{\|f\|,\frac{|f(p)|}{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}\} = 1-\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. In particular, $|f(p)| \leq (1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ for all $p \in F$. Extend the domain of $f$ to all of $X$ without increasing the Lipschitz norm using the McShane extension theorem, and call this extension $f'$. Define $F_+ := \{p \in F: f(p) > 0\}$ and $F_- := \{p \in F: f(p) < 0\}$. Define $g_+,g_-: X \to \mathbb{R}$ by $g_+(x) = \max_{p \in F_+} \{0,(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-d(p,x)\}$ and $g_-(x) = -\max_{p \in F_-} \{0,(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-d(p,x)\}$. Then $\|g_+\|,\|g_-\| \leq 1$, $g_+ \geq 0$, $g_- \leq 0$, and $\supp{g_+} \subseteq \cup_{p \in F_+} B_{(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}(p)$ and $\supp{g_-} \subseteq \cup_{p \in F_-} B_{(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}(p)$. Then $f'' := \max(g_-,\min(g_+,f'))$ satisfies $\|f''\| \leq 1$ and $\supp{f} \subseteq \cup_{p \in F} B_{(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}(p)$ which belongs to $\mathcal{I}$ since it is a finite union of sets which themselves belong to $\mathcal{I}$ by definition of $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. Also, the condition $|f(p)| \leq (1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ for all $p \in F$ implies $f''(p) = f(p)$ for all $p \in F$. This implies $T(f'') = (f,\sum_{p \in F} f(p)\mathsf{1}_p)$, proving that $T$ is a quotient map.
nodes.statement_short: Show T is a quotient onto V.

nodes.name: Contractivity
nodes.statement: Linearity is clear, and contractivity is as well as soon one recalls (from the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:radInorm}) that $|f(p)| \leq \|f\|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ whenever $f \in \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: Use $|f(p)| \le \|f\| rad_I(p)$.

nodes.name: Element of V
nodes.statement: Now let $(f,\sum_{p \in F} f(p)\mathsf{1}_p) \in V$ with $\max_{p \in F} \{\|f\|,\frac{|f(p)|}{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}\} = 1-\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. In particular, $|f(p)| \leq (1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ for all $p \in F$.
nodes.statement_short: Take an element of norm $1-\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: McShane extension and tents
nodes.statement: Extend the domain of $f$ to all of $X$ without increasing the Lipschitz norm using the McShane extension theorem, and call this extension $f'$. Define $F_+ := \{p \in F: f(p) > 0\}$ and $F_- := \{p \in F: f(p) < 0\}$. Define $g_+,g_-: X \to \mathbb{R}$ by $g_+(x) = \max_{p \in F_+} \{0,(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-d(p,x)\}$ and $g_-(x) = -\max_{p \in F_-} \{0,(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-d(p,x)\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend f and define tent caps $g_\pm$.

nodes.name: Truncated extension
nodes.statement: Then $\|g_+\|,\|g_-\| \leq 1$, $g_+ \geq 0$, $g_- \leq 0$, and $\supp{g_+} \subseteq \cup_{p \in F_+} B_{(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}(p)$ and $\supp{g_-} \subseteq \cup_{p \in F_-} B_{(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}(p)$. Then $f'' := \max(g_-,\min(g_+,f'))$ satisfies $\|f''\| \leq 1$ and $\supp{f} \subseteq \cup_{p \in F} B_{(1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}}(p)$ which belongs to $\mathcal{I}$ since it is a finite union of sets which themselves belong to $\mathcal{I}$ by definition of $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. Also, the condition $|f(p)| \leq (1-\varepsilon)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$ for all $p \in F$ implies $f''(p) = f(p)$ for all $p \in F$.
nodes.statement_short: Truncation f'' has norm ≤1, support in I and agrees with f on F.

nodes.name: T is a quotient
nodes.statement: This implies $T(f'') = (f,\sum_{p \in F} f(p)\mathsf{1}_p)$, proving that $T$ is a quotient map.
nodes.statement_short: f'' is a preimage, so T is a quotient.

nodes.name: Adjoint is isometric
nodes.statement: $T^*: V^* \to \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}^*$ is then an isometric embedding. The image of $T^*$ is exactly the subspace of $\LFf{\mathcal{I}}{X} \subseteq \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}^*$ consisting of elements supported in $F$. In particular, $v \in \mathrm{im}(T^*)$.
nodes.statement_short: v lies in the image of the isometric adjoint.

nodes.name: Lift v
nodes.statement: Since $V \subseteq \Lip{F} \oplus_\infty \ell^\infty_{\mathcal{I}}(F)$, there is a quotient map $S: \LF{F} \oplus_1 \l{\mathcal{I}}{F} \twoheadrightarrow V^*$ so that $T^* \circ S: \LF{F} \oplus_1 \l{\mathcal{I}}{F} \to \mathrm{im}(T^*)$ is a quotient map. Then since $v \in \mathrm{im}(T^*)$ with $\|v\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$, there are $w \in \LF{F} \subseteq \LF{Y}$ and $a \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{F} \subseteq \l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ such that $T^*(S(w,a)) = v$ and $\|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{F}} < 1$. It is easily seen that $T^*(S(w,a)) = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a)$, proving the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Compose with a quotient S to lift v to (w,a) of norm <1.

nodes.name: Injectivity of R^{ulm(I)}_I
nodes.statement: For every ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$, $R^{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}}: \LF{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{X} \to \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ is injective.
nodes.label: thm:injective

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.13
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal. Let $v \in \ker(R^{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}})$. Let \\ $f \in B_{\Lip{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{X}}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ be arbitrary. Set $A := \supp{f} \in \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$. Let $\theta > 0$ such that $A \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{I}$ for every $F \subseteq X$ finite. Choose $w \in \LFf{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{X}$ such that $F := \supp{w}$ is finite and $\|v-w\|_{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}} < \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1}$. Set $\tilde{f} := T^*_{F,\theta}(f)$. Then Proposition \ref{prop:T} implies $w(\tilde{f}) = w(f)$ and $\|\tilde{f}\| \leq C(\theta)$. Furthermore, $\supp{\tilde{f}} = A \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{I}$, so $\tilde{f} \in \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$. Then since $R^{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v) = 0$, $v(\tilde{f}) = 0$. Putting these together we get $$|v(f)| \leq \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1}\|f\| + |w(f)| = \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1}\|f\| + |w(\tilde{f})| \leq \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1} + |w(\tilde{f})|$$ $$\leq \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1} + \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1}\|\tilde{f}\| + |v(\tilde{f})| = \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1} + \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1}\|\tilde{f}\|$$ $$\leq \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1} + \varepsilon \leq 2\varepsilon.$$ Since $f \in B_{\Lip{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{X}}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ were arbitrary, this shows $v = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate v by finitely supported w and cut off any test function f by $T^*_{F,\theta}$ to land in Lip(I,X), where v vanishes.

nodes.name: Fix v, f, epsilon, theta
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal. Let $v \in \ker(R^{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}})$. Let \\ $f \in B_{\Lip{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{X}}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ be arbitrary. Set $A := \supp{f} \in \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$. Let $\theta > 0$ such that $A \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{I}$ for every $F \subseteq X$ finite.
nodes.statement_short: Take v in the kernel, test function f, and uniform radius $\theta$.

nodes.name: Approximant and cut-off
nodes.statement: Choose $w \in \LFf{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{X}$ such that $F := \supp{w}$ is finite and $\|v-w\|_{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}} < \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1}$. Set $\tilde{f} := T^*_{F,\theta}(f)$.
nodes.statement_short: Finitely supported approximant w and $\tilde f = T^*_{F,\theta}f$.

nodes.name: Cut-off lies in Lip(I,X)
nodes.statement: Then Proposition \ref{prop:T} implies $w(\tilde{f}) = w(f)$ and $\|\tilde{f}\| \leq C(\theta)$. Furthermore, $\supp{\tilde{f}} = A \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{I}$, so $\tilde{f} \in \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: Prop 4.2: $\tilde f$ agrees with f on supp w, bounded, supported in I.

nodes.name: Estimate v(f)
nodes.statement: Then since $R^{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v) = 0$, $v(\tilde{f}) = 0$. Putting these together we get $$|v(f)| \leq \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1}\|f\| + |w(f)| = \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1}\|f\| + |w(\tilde{f})| \leq \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1} + |w(\tilde{f})|$$ $$\leq \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1} + \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1}\|\tilde{f}\| + |v(\tilde{f})| = \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1} + \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1}\|\tilde{f}\|$$ $$\leq \varepsilon C(\theta)^{-1} + \varepsilon \leq 2\varepsilon.$$
nodes.statement_short: $v(\tilde f)=0$, so $|v(f)| \le 2\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: v = 0
nodes.statement: Since $f \in B_{\Lip{\ulm{\mathcal{I}}}{X}}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ were arbitrary, this shows $v = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Arbitrariness gives v = 0.

nodes.name: Ideal generated by A and I
nodes.statement: For a closed subset $A \subseteq X$ and ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$, we let $\boldsymbol{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ denote the ideal generated by $A$ and $\mathcal{I}$. Precisely, $\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle := \{B \cup I: \Cl{X} \ni B \subseteq A, I \in \mathcal{I}\}$. We define $\boldsymbol{\langle A \rangle}$ to be the ideal generated by $A$, meaning the collection of closed subsets of $A$.

nodes.name: Restriction isomorphism for A in ulm(I)
nodes.statement: For every ideal $\mathcal{I}$ and $A \in \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$, $R^{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}}: \LF{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}{X} \to \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.label: lem:isomorphism

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.15
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal and $A \in \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$. Clearly $\mathrm{im}(R^{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}})$ contains the dense subset $\LFf{\mathcal{I}}{X} \subseteq \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$. Let $\theta > 0$ such that $A \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{I}$ for every $F \subseteq X$ finite. Let $v \in \LFf{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}{X}$ with finite support $F := \supp{v}$. Let $f \in B_{\Lip{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}{X}}$ such that $|v(f)| \geq \|v\|_{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}/2$. Let $I \in \mathcal{I}$ such that $\supp{f} \subseteq A \cup I$. Then by Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $\supp{T^*_{F,\theta}(f)} \subseteq \supp{f} \cap B_\theta(F) \subseteq (A \cap B_\theta(F)) \cup I \in \mathcal{I}$, and thus $T^*_{F,\theta}(f) \in \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$. Also by Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $\|T^*_{F,\theta}(f)\|$ is bounded by some function of $\theta$, $C(\theta)$ (independent of $f$). Note $T^*_{F,\theta}(f)$ agrees with $f$ on $F$ and so $R^{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}}(v)(T^*_{F,\theta}(f)) = v(f)$. Putting this all together we get $$\|R^{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}}(v)\|_{\mathcal{I}} \geq C(\theta)^{-1}|R^{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}}(v)(T^*_{F,\theta}(f))| = C(\theta)^{-1}|v(f)| \geq \frac{C(\theta)^{-1}}{2}\|v\|_{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Dense range is clear; the lower bound follows by cutting off a norming function with $T^*_{F,\theta}$, losing only a factor $C(\theta)$.

nodes.name: Dense range
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ be an ideal and $A \in \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$. Clearly $\mathrm{im}(R^{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}})$ contains the dense subset $\LFf{\mathcal{I}}{X} \subseteq \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: The image contains a dense subset.

nodes.name: Fix theta, v, f, I
nodes.statement: Let $\theta > 0$ such that $A \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{I}$ for every $F \subseteq X$ finite. Let $v \in \LFf{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}{X}$ with finite support $F := \supp{v}$. Let $f \in B_{\Lip{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}{X}}$ such that $|v(f)| \geq \|v\|_{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}/2$. Let $I \in \mathcal{I}$ such that $\supp{f} \subseteq A \cup I$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform radius, finitely supported v, almost-norming f.

nodes.name: Cut-off in Lip(I,X)
nodes.statement: Then by Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $\supp{T^*_{F,\theta}(f)} \subseteq \supp{f} \cap B_\theta(F) \subseteq (A \cap B_\theta(F)) \cup I \in \mathcal{I}$, and thus $T^*_{F,\theta}(f) \in \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$. Also by Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $\|T^*_{F,\theta}(f)\|$ is bounded by some function of $\theta$, $C(\theta)$ (independent of $f$).
nodes.statement_short: Prop 4.2: the cut-off lies in Lip(I,X) with norm ≤ C(θ).

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement: Note $T^*_{F,\theta}(f)$ agrees with $f$ on $F$ and so $R^{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}}(v)(T^*_{F,\theta}(f)) = v(f)$. Putting this all together we get $$\|R^{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}}(v)\|_{\mathcal{I}} \geq C(\theta)^{-1}|R^{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}}(v)(T^*_{F,\theta}(f))| = C(\theta)^{-1}|v(f)| \geq \frac{C(\theta)^{-1}}{2}\|v\|_{\langle A,\mathcal{I} \rangle}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Restriction norm ≥ $C(\theta)^{-1}/2 \|v\|$.

nodes.name: Decomposition with short jumps
nodes.statement: For any ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$, $Y \subseteq X$, $c \in (0,1)$, and $u \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ with $\|u\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$ there exist, setting $\rho(p,q) := c \min\{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}\}$, $\{b_{(p,q)}\}_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}$, and $\{\tilde{a}_p\}_{p \in Y} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that $$u = \sum_{\substack{(p,q) \in Y^2 \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in Y} \tilde{a}_{p} \delta_p$$ and $$\sum_{\substack{(p,q) \in Y^2 \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in Y} |\tilde{a}_{p}|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} < 3c^{-1}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Any u in the unit ball of LF(I,Y) decomposes into short molecules (jumps $\le c\min rad$) plus point masses, with total weight $< 3/c$.
nodes.label: lem:quotientclose

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.16
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I}$, $Y$, $c$, $u$, be as above. First we show that whenever $p,q \in X$ such that $d(p,q) > \rho(p,q) = c\cdot \min\{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}\}$, it holds that \begin{equation} \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} < 3c^{-1}d(p,q). \end{equation} Let $p,q$ be such points, and without loss of generality assume $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. So then we have $d(p,q) > c \cdot \rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$ and thus $2c^{-1}d(p,q)>2\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$. It is also an immediate consequence of the triangle inequality and the definition of rad${_{\mathcal{I}}}$ that $d(p,q) \geq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$. Adding these two inequalities, and using the fact that $c \leq 1$, gives us $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} < 3c^{-1}d(p,q)$. Now, by Theorem \ref{thm:quotient}, there are $w \in \LF{Y}$ and $a \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ such that $R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a) = u$ and $\|w\|+\|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}} < 1$. Suppose $w = \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2} b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q)$ with $\sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}} < 1$. Set $$\tilde{a} := a + \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) > \rho(p,q)} b_{(p,q)}(\mathsf{1}_p-\mathsf{1}_q).$$ The following estimate will show that $\tilde{a}$ is a well-defined element of $\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ and moreover that $\sum_{(p,q): d(p,q) \in Y^2 \leq \rho(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in Y} |\tilde{a}_{p}|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} < 3c^{-1}.$ $$\sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in Y} |\tilde{a}_{p}|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$$ $$\leq \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q)$$ $$+ \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}} + \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) > \rho(p,q)} |b_{(p,q)}|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})$$ $$\overset{\eqref{eq:3c-1}}{\leq} \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}} + \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) > \rho(p,q)} |b_{(p,q)}|3c^{-1}d(p,q)$$ $$\leq 3c^{-1}\left(\sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}}\right) < 3c^{-1}.$$ It is obvious that $$u = \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in Y} \tilde{a}_{p} \delta_p,$$ proving the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Long jumps are cheap to replace by point masses since $rad(p)+rad(q) < 3c^{-1}d(p,q)$; apply Theorem 6.12 and move long-jump terms into $\tilde a$.

nodes.name: Claim: long jumps bound
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I}$, $Y$, $c$, $u$, be as above. First we show that whenever $p,q \in X$ such that $d(p,q) > \rho(p,q) = c\cdot \min\{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}\}$, it holds that \begin{equation} \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} < 3c^{-1}d(p,q). \end{equation} Let $p,q$ be such points, and without loss of generality assume $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. So then we have $d(p,q) > c \cdot \rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$ and thus $2c^{-1}d(p,q)>2\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$. It is also an immediate consequence of the triangle inequality and the definition of rad${_{\mathcal{I}}}$ that $d(p,q) \geq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$. Adding these two inequalities, and using the fact that $c \leq 1$, gives us $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} < 3c^{-1}d(p,q)$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $rad(p)+rad(q) < 3c^{-1}d(p,q)$ for long jumps.

nodes.name: WLOG and first inequality
nodes.statement: Let $p,q$ be such points, and without loss of generality assume $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. So then we have $d(p,q) > c \cdot \rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$ and thus $2c^{-1}d(p,q)>2\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$. It is also an immediate consequence of the triangle inequality and the definition of rad${_{\mathcal{I}}}$ that $d(p,q) \geq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG rad(q) ≤ rad(p); triangle inequality bounds the difference.

nodes.name: Add inequalities
nodes.statement: Adding these two inequalities, and using the fact that $c \leq 1$, gives us $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} < 3c^{-1}d(p,q)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum gives the bound.

nodes.name: Apply quotient theorem
nodes.statement: Now, by Theorem \ref{thm:quotient}, there are $w \in \LF{Y}$ and $a \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ such that $R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a) = u$ and $\|w\|+\|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}} < 1$. Suppose $w = \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2} b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q)$ with $\sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}} < 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Get w, a and a molecular representation of w.

nodes.name: Move long jumps
nodes.statement: Set $$\tilde{a} := a + \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) > \rho(p,q)} b_{(p,q)}(\mathsf{1}_p-\mathsf{1}_q).$$
nodes.statement_short: Define $\tilde a$ absorbing long-jump terms.

nodes.name: Weight estimate
nodes.statement: The following estimate will show that $\tilde{a}$ is a well-defined element of $\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ and moreover that $\sum_{(p,q): d(p,q) \in Y^2 \leq \rho(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in Y} |\tilde{a}_{p}|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} < 3c^{-1}.$ $$\sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in Y} |\tilde{a}_{p}|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$$ $$\leq \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q)$$ $$+ \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}} + \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) > \rho(p,q)} |b_{(p,q)}|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})$$ $$\overset{\eqref{eq:3c-1}}{\leq} \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}} + \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) > \rho(p,q)} |b_{(p,q)}|3c^{-1}d(p,q)$$ $$\leq 3c^{-1}\left(\sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}}\right) < 3c^{-1}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Use the claim to bound total weight by $3/c$.

nodes.name: Representation of u
nodes.statement: It is obvious that $$u = \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in Y} \tilde{a}_{p} \delta_p,$$ proving the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: The new representation equals u.

nodes.name: Long-jump radius bound
nodes.statement: \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} < 3c^{-1}d(p,q).
nodes.label: eq:3c-1

nodes.name: Decomposition with sign separation
nodes.statement: For every ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ and $u \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ with $\|u\| < 1$, there exist $\tilde{w} \in \LF{X}$ and $\tilde{a} \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $u = R_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{w}) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{a})$, $\|\tilde{w}\| + \|\tilde{a}\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} < 1$, and the following separation property is satisfied: whenever $\tilde{a}_p \cdot \tilde{a}_q < 0$ for some $p \neq q \in X$, then $d(p,q) \geq (\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})/2$.
conclusions: there exist $\tilde{w} \in \LF{X}$ and $\tilde{a} \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $u = R_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{w}) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{a})$, $\|\tilde{w}\| + \|\tilde{a}\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} < 1$, and the following separation property is satisfied: whenever $\tilde{a}_p \cdot \tilde{a}_q < 0$ for some $p \neq q \in X$, then $d(p,q) \geq (\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})/2$
nodes.statement_short: Representations from Theorem 6.12 can be chosen so that point masses of opposite sign are far apart relative to their radii.
nodes.label: lem:quotientseparated

|	ilde{a}_q|(ad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+ad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$+ |	ilde{a}_q+	ilde{a}_p|ad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}|	ilde{a}_s|ad{\mathcal{I}}{s}$$ $$= \|	ilde{w}\|-	ilde{a}_q(ad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+ad{\mathcal{I}}{q}) - |	ilde{a}_q|(ad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+ad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$+ (	ilde{a}_q+	ilde{a}_p)ad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}|	ilde{a}_s|ad{\mathcal{I}}{s}$$ $$= \|	ilde{w}\|+\sum_{s \in X}|	ilde{a}_s|ad{\mathcal{I}}{s} - |	ilde{a}_q|(ad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+ad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$= \|	ilde{w}\|+\|	ilde{a}\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} - |	ilde{a}_q|(ad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+ad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$\leq \|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$ - \sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|(ad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+ad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha}-d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha)) - |	ilde{a}_q|(ad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+ad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ where the last inequality follows from (ef{item:14}) applied to the family $\{(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A}$ (the maximal family given to us by Zorn's lemma). This shows (ef{item:14}). Finally, we use (ef{item:14}) to verify (ef{item:13}).
