nodes.name: Initial decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{I}$ and $u$ be as above. By Theorem \ref{thm:quotient}, there exist $w \in \LF{X}$ and $a \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $u = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a)$ and $\|w\|+\|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} < 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 6.12 gives w, a.

nodes.name: Families of transfers
nodes.statement: Set $\tilde{X} := X \times X \setminus \Delta$, where $\Delta$ is the diagonal. Consider a family of triples $\{(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A} \subseteq \mathbb{R} \times \tilde{X}$ indexed by a countable ordinal $A$ satisfying \begin{enumerate} \item $c_\alpha \neq 0$ for all $\alpha \in A$, \item $d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha) < (\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha})/2$ for all $\alpha \in A$, \item $\sum_{\alpha \in A} \|c_\alpha(\delta_{p_\alpha}-\delta_{q_\alpha})\| = \sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha) \leq 1$ and \\ $\sum_{\alpha \in A} \left\|c_\alpha(\mathsf{1}_{p_\alpha}-\mathsf{1}_{q_\alpha})\right\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} = \sum_{\alpha \in A}, |c_\alpha|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha}) \leq 2$ \item
nodes.statement_short: Consider countable families of triples satisfying conditions (1)-(3).

nodes.name: Condition (4)
nodes.statement: $\|w+x\| + \|a-y\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} \leq \|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} - \sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha}-d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha))$, where $x := \sum_{\alpha \in A}c_\alpha(\delta_{p_\alpha}-\delta_{q_\alpha}) \in \LF{X}$ and $y := \sum_{\alpha \in A} c_\alpha(\mathsf{1}_{p_\alpha}-\mathsf{1}_{q_\alpha}) \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ ($x$ and $y$ are well-defined by (\ref{item:13})). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Norm decrease condition (4).

nodes.name: Zorn's lemma
nodes.statement: The collection of all such indexed families is a poset under the relation $\{(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A} \leq \{(b_\beta,r_\beta,s_\beta)\}_{\beta \in B}$ if $A \subseteq B$ and for all $\alpha \in A$, $(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha) = (b_\alpha,r_\alpha,s_\alpha)$. This collection is obviously nonempty since it contains $\emptyset$ (and it is a set since we require the indexing sets to be countable ordinals). Every chain is bounded above by the union of the families in the chain. This union belongs to our poset since the four items above are all preserved under limits and items (\ref{item:11}) and (\ref{item:13}) and the fact that $p_\alpha \neq q_\alpha$ for all $\alpha \in A$ imply the indexing set must be countable. Thus we get a maximal element $\{(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A}$ by Zorn's lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Chains have upper bounds; take a maximal family.

nodes.name: Define tilde w, tilde a
nodes.statement: Set $\tilde{x} := \sum_{\alpha \in A}c_\alpha(\delta_{p_\alpha}-\delta_{q_\alpha}) \in \LF{X}$ and $\tilde{y} := \sum_{\alpha \in A} c_\alpha(\mathsf{1}_{p_\alpha}-\mathsf{1}_{q_\alpha}) \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$. Set $\tilde{w} := w + \tilde{x}$ and $\tilde{a} := a - \tilde{y}$. We complete the proof by showing that $\tilde{w},\tilde{a}$ satisfy the three desired properties. Clearly $R_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{w}) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{a}) = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a) = u$, and (\ref{item:12}) and (\ref{item:14}) imply $\|\tilde{w}\|+\|\tilde{a}\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} \leq \|w\|+\|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$. Since $\|w\|+\|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} < 1$, it only remains to show the separation property.
nodes.statement_short: Define the corrected decomposition; only separation remains.

nodes.name: Assume separation fails
nodes.statement: Suppose that it does not hold. Let $p \neq q \in X$ such that $\tilde{a}_p \cdot \tilde{a}_q < 0$ and $d(p,q) < (\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})/2$. Without loss of generality, we may assume $\tilde{a}_p > 0$ and $\tilde{a}_q < 0$. Then there are two cases: $|\tilde{a}_p| \geq |\tilde{a}_q|$ and $|\tilde{a}_p| \leq |\tilde{a}_q|$. We will assume the first case holds - the second case can be treated similarly. We consider the new family of triples $\{(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A} \cup \{(-\tilde{a}_q,p,q)\}$ indexed by the successor of $A$. If we can show this family belongs to our collection, this will contradict maximality. Items (\ref{item:11}) and (\ref{item:12}) clearly hold for this family. Next we verify (\ref{item:14}). Letting $x,y$ be as defined in (\ref{item:14}) for the family under consideration, we have $$\|w+x\| + \|a-y\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} = \|w+\tilde{x}-\tilde{a}_q(\delta_p-\delta_q)\| + \|a-\tilde{y}+\tilde{a}_q(\mathsf{1}_p-\mathsf{1}_q)\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}-\tilde{a}_q(\delta_p-\delta_q)\| + \|\tilde{a}+\tilde{a}_q(\mathsf{1}_p-\mathsf{1}_q)\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}-\tilde{a}_q(\delta_p-\delta_q)\| + \left\|(\tilde{a}_q+\tilde{a}_p)\mathsf{1}_p+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}\tilde{a}_s\mathsf{1}_s\right\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$\leq \|\tilde{w}\|+|\tilde{a}_q|d(p,q) + \left\|(\tilde{a}_q+\tilde{a}_p)\mathsf{1}_p+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}\tilde{a}_s\mathsf{1}_s\right\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}\|+|\tilde{a}_q|d(p,q) + |\tilde{a}_q+\tilde{a}_p|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}|\tilde{a}_s|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{s}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}\|+|\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}) - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$+ |\tilde{a}_q+\tilde{a}_p|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}|\tilde{a}_s|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{s}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}\|-\tilde{a}_q(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}) - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$+ (\tilde{a}_q+\tilde{a}_p)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}|\tilde{a}_s|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{s}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}\|+\sum_{s \in X}|\tilde{a}_s|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{s} - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}\|+\|\tilde{a}\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$\leq \|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$ - \sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha}-d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha)) - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ where the last inequality follows from (\ref{item:14}) applied to the family $\{(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A}$ (the maximal family given to us by Zorn's lemma). This shows (\ref{item:14}).
nodes.statement_short: Derive contradiction with maximality.

nodes.name: Bad pair
nodes.statement: Suppose that it does not hold. Let $p \neq q \in X$ such that $\tilde{a}_p \cdot \tilde{a}_q < 0$ and $d(p,q) < (\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})/2$. Without loss of generality, we may assume $\tilde{a}_p > 0$ and $\tilde{a}_q < 0$. Then there are two cases: $|\tilde{a}_p| \geq |\tilde{a}_q|$ and $|\tilde{a}_p| \leq |\tilde{a}_q|$. We will assume the first case holds - the second case can be treated similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Take p, q with opposite signs too close; WLOG first case.

nodes.name: Extended family
nodes.statement: We consider the new family of triples $\{(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A} \cup \{(-\tilde{a}_q,p,q)\}$ indexed by the successor of $A$. If we can show this family belongs to our collection, this will contradict maximality.
nodes.statement_short: Add the triple $(-\tilde a_q, p, q)$.

nodes.name: Items (1),(2)
nodes.statement: Items (\ref{item:11}) and (\ref{item:12}) clearly hold for this family.
nodes.statement_short: Trivially satisfied.

nodes.name: Verify (4)
nodes.statement: Next we verify (\ref{item:14}). Letting $x,y$ be as defined in (\ref{item:14}) for the family under consideration, we have $$\|w+x\| + \|a-y\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} = \|w+\tilde{x}-\tilde{a}_q(\delta_p-\delta_q)\| + \|a-\tilde{y}+\tilde{a}_q(\mathsf{1}_p-\mathsf{1}_q)\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}-\tilde{a}_q(\delta_p-\delta_q)\| + \|\tilde{a}+\tilde{a}_q(\mathsf{1}_p-\mathsf{1}_q)\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}-\tilde{a}_q(\delta_p-\delta_q)\| + \left\|(\tilde{a}_q+\tilde{a}_p)\mathsf{1}_p+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}\tilde{a}_s\mathsf{1}_s\right\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$\leq \|\tilde{w}\|+|\tilde{a}_q|d(p,q) + \left\|(\tilde{a}_q+\tilde{a}_p)\mathsf{1}_p+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}\tilde{a}_s\mathsf{1}_s\right\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}\|+|\tilde{a}_q|d(p,q) + |\tilde{a}_q+\tilde{a}_p|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}|\tilde{a}_s|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{s}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}\|+|\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}) - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$+ |\tilde{a}_q+\tilde{a}_p|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}|\tilde{a}_s|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{s}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}\|-\tilde{a}_q(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}) - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$+ (\tilde{a}_q+\tilde{a}_p)\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\sum_{s \in X \setminus \{p,q\}}|\tilde{a}_s|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{s}$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}\|+\sum_{s \in X}|\tilde{a}_s|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{s} - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$= \|\tilde{w}\|+\|\tilde{a}\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$\leq \|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$ - \sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha}-d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha)) - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ where the last inequality follows from (\ref{item:14}) applied to the family $\{(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A}$ (the maximal family given to us by Zorn's lemma). This shows (\ref{item:14}).
nodes.statement_short: Norm computation shows (4) holds for the extended family.

nodes.name: Verify (3)
nodes.statement: Finally, we use (\ref{item:14}) to verify (\ref{item:13}). We have $$0 \leq \|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$$ $$- \sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha}-d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha)) - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$\leq 1 - \sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha}-d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha)) - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}-d(p,q))$$ $$\leq 1 - \sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha})/2 - |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})/2,$$ which gives us $$\sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha) + |\tilde{a}_q|d(p,q)$$ $$\leq \sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha})/2 + |\tilde{a}_q|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})/2 \leq 1.$$
nodes.statement_short: (4) implies (3), contradicting maximality.

nodes.name: Decomposition with locally finite point masses
nodes.statement: Assume $X$ is countable with enumeration $X = \{p_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$. Fix an ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ and set $\mathcal{J} := \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$. For every $u \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ with $\|u\| < 1$ and collection of radii $\{r_p\}_{p \in X}$ with $r_p \in (0,\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p})$, there exist $w \in \LF{X}$ and $a \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $u = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a)$, $\|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} < 1$, and $\supp{a} \cap B_{r_p}(p)$ is finite for each $p \in X$.
conclusions: there exist $w \in \LF{X}$ and $a \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $u = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a)$, $\|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} < 1$, and $\supp{a} \cap B_{r_p}(p)$ is finite for each $p \in X$
nodes.statement_short: For countable X, decompositions can be chosen whose point-mass part is finitely supported in each ball $B_{r_p}(p)$.
nodes.label: lem:quotientfinite

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.18
nodes.statement: Let $u$ and $r_p$ be as above. By Lemma \ref{lem:quotientseparated}, there exist $w' \in \LF{X}$ and $a' \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $u = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w') + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a')$, $\|w'\|+\|a'\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} < 1$, and whenever $a'_p \cdot a'_q < 0$ for some $p \neq q \in X$, then $d(p,q) \geq (\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})/2$. Let $i \geq 1$. Since $r_{p_i} < \rad{\mathcal{J}}{p_i}$, Proposition \ref{prop:radIinf} implies \\ $\inf_{q \in B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)} \rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} \geq \theta$ for some $\theta > 0$. Set $S^+ := \{p \in X: a'_p > 0\}$ and $S^- := \{p \in X: a'_p < 0\}$. Let $F \subseteq (S^+ \cup S^-) \cap B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)$ be an arbitrary finite subset. Consider the functions $f^+,f^-: X \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f^+(x) = \max(0,1-2\theta^{-1}d(F \cap S^+,x))$ and $f^-(x) = \max(0,1-2\theta^{-1}d(F \cap S^-,x))$. We make several observations. \begin{itemize} \item $\supp{f^+} \cup \supp{f^-} \subseteq \cup_{q \in F} B_{\theta/2}(q)$. This is a finite union of sets in $\mathcal{I}$ and is thus itself in $\mathcal{I}$. \item $\|f^+\|,\|f^-\| \leq 2\theta^{-1}$. \item $\mathrm{im}(f^+),\mathrm{im}(f^-) \subseteq [0,1]$. \item $f^+(q) = 1$ for all $q \in F \cap S^+$ and $f^-(q) = 1$ for all $q \in F \cap S^-$. \item Since $d(p,q) \geq (\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})/2$ whenever $a'_p \cdot a'_q < 0$, $\supp{f^+} \cap S^- = \supp{f^-} \cap S^+ = \emptyset$. \end{itemize} Together these imply $$4\theta^{-1} \geq \|f^+-f^-\|\|Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a')\|_{\mathcal{I}} \geq |Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a')(f^+-f^-)| = \left|\sum_{q \in \supp{a'}} a'_q(f^+(q)-f^-(q))\right|$$ $$= \left|\sum_{q \in S^+} a'_qf^+(q) + \sum_{q \in S^-} (-a'_q)f^-(q)\right| = \sum_{q \in S^+} |a'_q|f^+(q) + \sum_{q \in S^-} |a'_q|f^-(q)$$ $$\geq \sum_{q \in F \cap S^+} |a'_q|f^+(q) + \sum_{q \in F \cap S^-} |a'_q|f^-(q) = \sum_{q \in F} |a'_q|.$$ Since $F \subseteq (S^+ \cup S^-) \cap B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)$ was arbitrary, we get $\sum_{q \in B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)} |a'_q| \leq 4\theta^{-1}$. Thus, there is some cofinite subset $CF_i \subseteq B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)$ such that $\sum_{q \in CF_i} |a'_q| < 2^{-i}\varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon$ is any number in $(0,1-\|w'\|-\|a'\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}})$. Then setting $CF_\infty := \cup_{i=1}^\infty CF_i$, we get $\sum_{q \in CF_\infty} |a'_q| \leq \varepsilon$. Then we set $w := w' + \sum_{q \in CF_\infty} a'_q\delta_q$ and $a := \sum_{q \in X \setminus CF_\infty} a'_q\mathsf{1}_q \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$. Then $R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a) = R_I(w') + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a') = u$, $\|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} \leq \|w'\| + \varepsilon + \|a'\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} < 1$, and $\supp{a} \cap B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i) \subseteq B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i) \setminus CF_i$ for each $i \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Start from a sign-separated decomposition; tent functions show the point masses are summable in each ball, so cofinite tails can be moved into the LF(X) part.

nodes.name: Sign-separated decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $u$ and $r_p$ be as above. By Lemma \ref{lem:quotientseparated}, there exist $w' \in \LF{X}$ and $a' \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $u = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w') + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a')$, $\|w'\|+\|a'\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} < 1$, and whenever $a'_p \cdot a'_q < 0$ for some $p \neq q \in X$, then $d(p,q) \geq (\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.17 gives w', a'.

nodes.name: Uniform radius
nodes.statement: Let $i \geq 1$. Since $r_{p_i} < \rad{\mathcal{J}}{p_i}$, Proposition \ref{prop:radIinf} implies \\ $\inf_{q \in B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)} \rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} \geq \theta$ for some $\theta > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Prop 6.10 gives $\theta$ bounding rad below in the ball.

nodes.name: Tent functions
nodes.statement: Set $S^+ := \{p \in X: a'_p > 0\}$ and $S^- := \{p \in X: a'_p < 0\}$. Let $F \subseteq (S^+ \cup S^-) \cap B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)$ be an arbitrary finite subset. Consider the functions $f^+,f^-: X \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f^+(x) = \max(0,1-2\theta^{-1}d(F \cap S^+,x))$ and $f^-(x) = \max(0,1-2\theta^{-1}d(F \cap S^-,x))$. We make several observations. \begin{itemize} \item
nodes.statement_short: Define sign sets, finite F, and tents $f^\pm$.

nodes.name: Supports in I
nodes.statement: $\supp{f^+} \cup \supp{f^-} \subseteq \cup_{q \in F} B_{\theta/2}(q)$. This is a finite union of sets in $\mathcal{I}$ and is thus itself in $\mathcal{I}$. \item
nodes.statement_short: Supports of the tents lie in I.

nodes.name: Norm and range bounds
nodes.statement: $\|f^+\|,\|f^-\| \leq 2\theta^{-1}$. \item $\mathrm{im}(f^+),\mathrm{im}(f^-) \subseteq [0,1]$. \item
nodes.statement_short: Tents have norm at most $2/\theta$ and values in [0,1].

nodes.name: Values and disjointness
nodes.statement: $f^+(q) = 1$ for all $q \in F \cap S^+$ and $f^-(q) = 1$ for all $q \in F \cap S^-$. \item Since $d(p,q) \geq (\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q})/2$ whenever $a'_p \cdot a'_q < 0$, $\supp{f^+} \cap S^- = \supp{f^-} \cap S^+ = \emptyset$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Tents equal 1 on F and, by separation, vanish on opposite-sign points.

nodes.name: Summability in the ball
nodes.statement: Together these imply $$4\theta^{-1} \geq \|f^+-f^-\|\|Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a')\|_{\mathcal{I}} \geq |Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a')(f^+-f^-)| = \left|\sum_{q \in \supp{a'}} a'_q(f^+(q)-f^-(q))\right|$$ $$= \left|\sum_{q \in S^+} a'_qf^+(q) + \sum_{q \in S^-} (-a'_q)f^-(q)\right| = \sum_{q \in S^+} |a'_q|f^+(q) + \sum_{q \in S^-} |a'_q|f^-(q)$$ $$\geq \sum_{q \in F \cap S^+} |a'_q|f^+(q) + \sum_{q \in F \cap S^-} |a'_q|f^-(q) = \sum_{q \in F} |a'_q|.$$ Since $F \subseteq (S^+ \cup S^-) \cap B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)$ was arbitrary, we get $\sum_{q \in B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)} |a'_q| \leq 4\theta^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum of $|a'_q|$ over the ball is at most $4/\theta$.

nodes.name: Move tails
nodes.statement: Thus, there is some cofinite subset $CF_i \subseteq B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i)$ such that $\sum_{q \in CF_i} |a'_q| < 2^{-i}\varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon$ is any number in $(0,1-\|w'\|-\|a'\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}})$. Then setting $CF_\infty := \cup_{i=1}^\infty CF_i$, we get $\sum_{q \in CF_\infty} |a'_q| \leq \varepsilon$. Then we set $w := w' + \sum_{q \in CF_\infty} a'_q\delta_q$ and $a := \sum_{q \in X \setminus CF_\infty} a'_q\mathsf{1}_q \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose cofinite tails of small mass and move them into w.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Then $R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a) = R_I(w') + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a') = u$, $\|w\| + \|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} \leq \|w'\| + \varepsilon + \|a'\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} < 1$, and $\supp{a} \cap B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i) \subseteq B_{r_{p_i}}(p_i) \setminus CF_i$ for each $i \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: New decomposition has the required properties.

nodes.name: Formal sums and supports in LF(I,X) for discrete X
nodes.statement: Recall that $\mathcal{F}in \subseteq \Cl{X}$ is the ideal of finite subsets of $X$. Suppose $X$ is discrete. Then for each $p \in X$, $\mathsf{1}_p \in \Lip{\mathcal{F}in}{X}$. For any $\lambda \in \Lip{\mathcal{F}in}{X}^*$, we write $\lambda = \sum_{p \in X} c_p\delta_p$ if $\lambda(\mathsf{1}_p) = c_p$ for each $p \in X$. This gives a well-defined linear injection $\Lip{\mathcal{F}in}{X}^* \to \mathbb{R}^{X}$. We emphasize that the notation is purely formal and that we make no attempt to interpret it as a limit of finite sums. Whenever $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ is an ideal such that $\mathcal{F}in \subseteq \mathcal{I}$ and $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}: \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X} \to \LF{\mathcal{F}in}{X}$ is injective and $v \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$, we also write $v = \sum_{p \in X} c_p\delta_p$ to mean $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(v) = \sum_{p \in X} c_p\delta_p$. Since $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective, this again gives a well-defined linear injection $\LF{\mathcal{I}}{X} \to \mathbb{R}^X$. For example, Theorem \ref{thm:injective} and induction imply $R^{\mathcal{F}in_n}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective for all $n \geq 0$. Whenever $v = \sum_{p \in X} c_p\delta_p$, we define $\boldsymbol{\supp{v}} := \{p \in X: c_p \neq 0\} = \{p \in X: v(\mathsf{1}_p) \neq 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: For discrete X, elements of LF(I,X) (with injective restriction to Fin) are identified with formal coefficient families; support is the set of nonzero coefficients.

nodes.name: Support conjecture: v lies in LF(I, supp v)
nodes.statement: A natural question is whether $v \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{\supp{v}}$. While we believe this is true, we prove only a very restricted version in Lemma \ref{lem:supp}.

nodes.name: Support localization lemma
nodes.statement: Assume $X$ is discrete. Fix an ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ such that $\mathcal{F}in \subseteq \mathcal{I}$ and $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective. For all $Y,F \subseteq X$ with $F$ finite, $v \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$, and $\varepsilon>0$, if $\supp{v} \subseteq Y \cup F$, then $v \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \cup F}$.
assumptions: an ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ such that $\mathcal{F}in \subseteq \mathcal{I}$ and $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective
nodes.label: lem:supp

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.20
nodes.statement: Let $Y,F,v,\varepsilon$ be as above. Assume $\supp{v} \subseteq Y \cup F$. Let $\psi': X \to [0,1]$ be a Lipschitz function equal to 1 on $Y$ and 0 on $X \setminus B_{\varepsilon}(Y)$. Since $F$ is finite and $X$ is discrete, $\mathsf{1}_F: X \to [0,1]$ is Lipschitz. Set $\psi := \max(\psi'+\mathsf{1}_F,1): X \to [0,1]$, so that $\psi$ is Lipschitz, equals 1 on $Y \cup F$, and equals 0 on $X \setminus (B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \cup F)$. The map $f \mapsto \psi \cdot f$ is a bounded linear operator $\Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X} \to \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$, and its dual $T: \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}^* \to \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}^*$ maps $\LFf{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ into $\LFf{\mathcal{I}}{B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \cup F}$ and thus also $\LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ into $\LF{\mathcal{I}}{B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \cup F}$. We will show $v = T(v)$, completing the proof because $T(v) \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \cup F}$. By hypothesis, $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective, so it suffices to show $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(v) = R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(T(v))$. Since $\{\mathsf{1}_p\}_{p \in X}$ spans $\Lip{\mathcal{F}in}{X}$, it suffices to show \\ $[R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(v)](\mathsf{1}_p) = [R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(T(v))](\mathsf{1}_p)$ for every $p \in X$. Let $p \in X$. We have $$[R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(v)](\mathsf{1}_p) = v(\mathsf{1}_p)$$ and $$[R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(T(v))](\mathsf{1}_p) = [T(v)](\mathsf{1}_p) = v(\psi \cdot \mathsf{1}_p) = \psi(p)v(\mathsf{1}_p)$$ so we need to show $v(\mathsf{1}_p) = \psi(p)v(\mathsf{1}_p)$. There are two cases to consider, $p \in \supp{v}$ and $p \in X \setminus \supp{v}$. In the first case, $\psi(p) = 1$ by definition of $\psi$ and the assumption $\supp{v} \subseteq Y \cup F$, and in the second case, $v(\mathsf{1}_p) = 0$ by definition of $\supp{v}$. In either case we have $v(\mathsf{1}_p) = \psi(p)v(\mathsf{1}_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by a Lipschitz cut-off $\psi$ equal to 1 on $Y\cup F$; its dual T maps into the localized space, and injectivity shows T(v) = v by testing on indicators.

nodes.name: Hypotheses
nodes.statement: Let $Y,F,v,\varepsilon$ be as above. Assume $\supp{v} \subseteq Y \cup F$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume supp v ⊆ Y ∪ F.

nodes.name: Cut-off psi
nodes.statement: Let $\psi': X \to [0,1]$ be a Lipschitz function equal to 1 on $Y$ and 0 on $X \setminus B_{\varepsilon}(Y)$. Since $F$ is finite and $X$ is discrete, $\mathsf{1}_F: X \to [0,1]$ is Lipschitz. Set $\psi := \max(\psi'+\mathsf{1}_F,1): X \to [0,1]$, so that $\psi$ is Lipschitz, equals 1 on $Y \cup F$, and equals 0 on $X \setminus (B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \cup F)$.
nodes.statement_short: Build Lipschitz $\psi$ equal to 1 on $Y\cup F$.

nodes.name: Dual multiplication operator
nodes.statement: The map $f \mapsto \psi \cdot f$ is a bounded linear operator $\Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X} \to \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$, and its dual $T: \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}^* \to \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}^*$ maps $\LFf{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ into $\LFf{\mathcal{I}}{B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \cup F}$ and thus also $\LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ into $\LF{\mathcal{I}}{B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \cup F}$.
nodes.statement_short: Its dual T maps into the localized space.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We will show $v = T(v)$, completing the proof because $T(v) \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \cup F}$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show v = T(v).

nodes.name: Reduce to indicators
nodes.statement: By hypothesis, $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective, so it suffices to show $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(v) = R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(T(v))$. Since $\{\mathsf{1}_p\}_{p \in X}$ spans $\Lip{\mathcal{F}in}{X}$, it suffices to show \\ $[R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(v)](\mathsf{1}_p) = [R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(T(v))](\mathsf{1}_p)$ for every $p \in X$.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity reduces to testing on $1_p$.

nodes.name: Compute on indicators
nodes.statement: Let $p \in X$. We have $$[R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(v)](\mathsf{1}_p) = v(\mathsf{1}_p)$$ and $$[R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}(T(v))](\mathsf{1}_p) = [T(v)](\mathsf{1}_p) = v(\psi \cdot \mathsf{1}_p) = \psi(p)v(\mathsf{1}_p)$$ so we need to show $v(\mathsf{1}_p) = \psi(p)v(\mathsf{1}_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Need $v(1_p) = \psi(p) v(1_p)$.

nodes.name: Two cases
nodes.statement: There are two cases to consider, $p \in \supp{v}$ and $p \in X \setminus \supp{v}$. In the first case, $\psi(p) = 1$ by definition of $\psi$ and the assumption $\supp{v} \subseteq Y \cup F$, and in the second case, $v(\mathsf{1}_p) = 0$ by definition of $\supp{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: p in supp v or not.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: In either case we have $v(\mathsf{1}_p) = \psi(p)v(\mathsf{1}_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Equality holds in both cases.

nodes.name: Support-reduction lemma in one ball
nodes.statement: Assume $X$ is discrete. Fix an ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ such that $\mathcal{F}in \subseteq \mathcal{I}$ and $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective. Set $\mathcal{J} := \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$ so that Theorem \ref{thm:injective} implies $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is also injective (for example, $\mathcal{I} = \mathcal{F}in_n$ and $\mathcal{J} = \mathcal{F}in_{n+1}$). For any $p \in X$, $r \in (0,\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p})$, $u \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $\supp{u} \cap B_{r}(p)$ is finite, and sequence $v_n \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$ such that $\sup_n \|v_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$ and $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v_n) \to u$, and $c \in (0,1)$, there exists another sequence $\tilde{v}_n$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $\sup_n \|\tilde{v}_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$, \item $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n) \to u$, \item $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \subseteq \supp{v_n}$, \item and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \cap B_{cr}(p) = \supp{u} \cap B_{cr}(p)$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: an ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ such that $\mathcal{F}in \subseteq \mathcal{I}$ and $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective
$p \in X$, $r \in (0,\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p})$, $u \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $\supp{u} \cap B_{r}(p)$ is finite
nodes.statement_short: Within a ball $B_{cr}(p)$, a sequence converging to u in the I-norm can be modified so its supports in the ball match supp u.
nodes.label: lem:sequence1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.21
nodes.statement:
Let $p,r,u,c$ be as above. Set $A_1 := B_{r}(p)$ and $A_2 := B_{cr}(p)$ so that $A_2 \subseteq A_1 \in \mathcal{J}$. Let $\psi$ be a Lipschitz bump function taking values in $[0,1]$, identically 1 on $A_2$, and 0 on $X \setminus A_1$ (for example, $\psi(q) = \max\{0,\min\{1,(1-c)^{-1}-(1-c)^{-1}r^{-1}d(p,q)\}\}$). The function $\psi$ induces a bounded linear operator $\Lip{A_1} 	o \Lip{\langle A_1 angle}{X}$ given by $f \mapsto \psi	ilde{f}$, where $	ilde{f}$ is any norm preserving extension of $f$ to all of $X$ (which exists by McShane). It's clear that this map does not depend on the choice of $	ilde{f}$, is linear, and has operator norm depending only on $c$ and $r$. The dual $T$ of this bounded operator maps $\LFf{\langle A_1 angle}{X}$ into $\LFf{A_1}$, and thus also $\LF{\langle A_1 angle}{X} into \LF{A_1} \subseteq \LF{X}$. Since $A_1 \in \mathcal{J} = \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$, Lemma ef{lem:isomorphism} implies $R^{\langle A_1,\mathcal{I} angle}_{\mathcal{I}}: \LF{\langle A_1,\mathcal{I} angle}{X} 	o \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ is an isomorphism. Thus, $S := R_{\mathcal{J}} \circ T \circ R^{\langle A_1,\mathcal{I} angle}_{\langle A_1 angle} \circ (R^{\langle A_1,\mathcal{I} angle}_{\mathcal{I}})^{-1}: \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X} 	o \LF{\mathcal{J},X}$ is a bounded linear map given by $$S\left(\sum_{q \in X} c_q\delta_qight) = \sum_{q \in X} c_q\psi(q)\delta_q = \sum_{q \in A_2} c_q\delta_q + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus A_2} c_q\psi(q)\delta_q.$$ Suppose $v_n = \sum_{p \in X} c_{p,n}\delta_p$ and $u = \sum_{p \in X} c_p\delta_p$. Then since $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v_n) 	o u$, $S(R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v_n)) 	o S(u) \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$, which translates to $$\sum_{q \in A_2} c_{q,n}\delta_{q} + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus A_2} c_{q,n}\psi(q)\delta_q 	o \sum_{q \in A_2} c_{q}\delta_{q} + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus A_2} c_{q}\psi(q)\delta_q \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}.$$ Set $F := \supp{u} \cap A_1$, which is finite by assumption. Since $X$ is discrete, $\mathsf{1}_q$ is a Lipschitz function for all $q \in X$ and hence $\sum_{q \in F} c_{q,n}\psi(q)\delta_q 	o \sum_{q \in F} c_{q}\psi(q)\delta_q \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$. Combining these implies $$\sum_{q \in A_2 \setminus F} c_{q,n}\delta_{q} + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus (A_2 \cup F)} c_{q,n}\psi(q)\delta_q 	o 0 \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}.$$ Choose $N$ large enough so that $$\left\| \sum_{q \in A_2 \setminus F} c_{q,n}\delta_{q} + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus (A_2 \cup F)} c_{q,n}\psi(q)\delta_q ight\|_{\mathcal{J}} <  rac{1 - \sup_n \|v_n\|}{2}$$ for all $n \geq N$. Then consider the $\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$-valued sequence $
u_n$ defined by $$
u_n = \left\{ egin{matrix} 0 & n < N \ \sum_{q \in A_2 \setminus F} c_{q,n}\delta_{q} + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus (A_2 \cup F)} c_{q,n}\psi(q)\delta_q & n \geq N \end{matrix}ight..$$ We have $\sup_n \|
u_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1 - \sup_n \|v_n\|$ and $\|
u_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} 	o 0$. Set $	ilde{v}_n := v_n - 
u_n$. Thus, $\sup_n \|	ilde{v}_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(	ilde{v}_n) 	o u$, $\supp{	ilde{v}_n} \subseteq \supp{v_n}$, and $\supp{	ilde{v}_n} \cap A_2 = F \cap A_2 = \supp{u} \cap A_2$ for all $n \geq N$. By omitting all the terms before $N$ and shifting the index, we may assume $\supp{	ilde{v}_n} \cap A_2 = \supp{u} \cap A_2$ for all $n \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: A bump function and Lemma 6.15 give a bounded map S upgrading I-convergence to J-convergence inside the ball; subtract the eventually small off-support part.

nodes.name: Balls and bump
nodes.statement: Let $p,r,u,c$ be as above. Set $A_1 := B_{r}(p)$ and $A_2 := B_{cr}(p)$ so that $A_2 \subseteq A_1 \in \mathcal{J}$. Let $\psi$ be a Lipschitz bump function taking values in $[0,1]$, identically 1 on $A_2$, and 0 on $X \setminus A_1$ (for example, $\psi(q) = \max\{0,\min\{1,(1-c)^{-1}-(1-c)^{-1}r^{-1}d(p,q)\}\}$).
nodes.statement_short: Set $A_1, A_2$ and bump $\psi$.

nodes.name: Multiplication operator
nodes.statement: The function $\psi$ induces a bounded linear operator $\Lip{A_1} \to \Lip{\langle A_1 \rangle}{X}$ given by $f \mapsto \psi\tilde{f}$, where $\tilde{f}$ is any norm preserving extension of $f$ to all of $X$ (which exists by McShane). It's clear that this map does not depend on the choice of $\tilde{f}$, is linear, and has operator norm depending only on $c$ and $r$. The dual $T$ of this bounded operator maps $\LFf{\langle A_1 \rangle}{X}$ into $\LFf{A_1}$, and thus also $\LF{\langle A_1 \rangle}{X} into \LF{A_1} \subseteq \LF{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bump induces bounded operator with dual T into LF(A_1).

nodes.name: Upgrade map S
nodes.statement: Since $A_1 \in \mathcal{J} = \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$, Lemma \ref{lem:isomorphism} implies $R^{\langle A_1,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}}: \LF{\langle A_1,\mathcal{I} \rangle}{X} \to \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ is an isomorphism. Thus, $S := R_{\mathcal{J}} \circ T \circ R^{\langle A_1,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\langle A_1 \rangle} \circ (R^{\langle A_1,\mathcal{I} \rangle}_{\mathcal{I}})^{-1}: \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X} \to \LF{\mathcal{J},X}$ is a bounded linear map given by $$S\left(\sum_{q \in X} c_q\delta_q\right) = \sum_{q \in X} c_q\psi(q)\delta_q = \sum_{q \in A_2} c_q\delta_q + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus A_2} c_q\psi(q)\delta_q.$$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.15 yields bounded $S: LF(I,X) \to LF(J,X)$.

nodes.name: Apply S
nodes.statement: Suppose $v_n = \sum_{p \in X} c_{p,n}\delta_p$ and $u = \sum_{p \in X} c_p\delta_p$. Then since $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v_n) \to u$, $S(R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v_n)) \to S(u) \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$, which translates to $$\sum_{q \in A_2} c_{q,n}\delta_{q} + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus A_2} c_{q,n}\psi(q)\delta_q \to \sum_{q \in A_2} c_{q}\delta_{q} + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus A_2} c_{q}\psi(q)\delta_q \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Convergence under S in the J-norm.

nodes.name: Off-support part tends to 0
nodes.statement: Set $F := \supp{u} \cap A_1$, which is finite by assumption. Since $X$ is discrete, $\mathsf{1}_q$ is a Lipschitz function for all $q \in X$ and hence $\sum_{q \in F} c_{q,n}\psi(q)\delta_q \to \sum_{q \in F} c_{q}\psi(q)\delta_q \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$. Combining these implies $$\sum_{q \in A_2 \setminus F} c_{q,n}\delta_{q} + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus (A_2 \cup F)} c_{q,n}\psi(q)\delta_q \to 0 \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Finite part converges, so the off-support part tends to 0.

nodes.name: Correction nu_n
nodes.statement:
Choose $N$ large enough so that $$\left\| \sum_{q \in A_2 \setminus F} c_{q,n}\delta_{q} + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus (A_2 \cup F)} c_{q,n}\psi(q)\delta_q ight\|_{\mathcal{J}} <  rac{1 - \sup_n \|v_n\|}{2}$$ for all $n \geq N$. Then consider the $\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$-valued sequence $
u_n$ defined by $$
u_n = \left\{ egin{matrix} 0 & n < N \ \sum_{q \in A_2 \setminus F} c_{q,n}\delta_{q} + \sum_{q \in A_1 \setminus (A_2 \cup F)} c_{q,n}\psi(q)\delta_q & n \geq N \end{matrix}ight..$$ We have $\sup_n \|
u_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1 - \sup_n \|v_n\|$ and $\|
u_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} 	o 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define small corrections $\nu_n$.

nodes.name: Corrected sequence
nodes.statement: Set $\tilde{v}_n := v_n - \nu_n$. Thus, $\sup_n \|\tilde{v}_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n) \to u$, $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \subseteq \supp{v_n}$, and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \cap A_2 = F \cap A_2 = \supp{u} \cap A_2$ for all $n \geq N$.
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde v_n$ has the required properties for n ≥ N.

nodes.name: Reindex
nodes.statement: By omitting all the terms before $N$ and shifting the index, we may assume $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \cap A_2 = \supp{u} \cap A_2$ for all $n \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Drop initial terms.

nodes.name: Support-reduction lemma in all balls
nodes.statement: Assume $X$ is countable with enumeration $X = \{p_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$. Assume $X$ is discrete. Fix an ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ such that $\mathcal{F}in \subseteq \mathcal{I}$ and $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective. Set $\mathcal{J} := \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$ so that Theorem \ref{thm:injective} implies $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is also injective (for example, $\mathcal{I} = \mathcal{F}in_n$ and $\mathcal{J} = \mathcal{F}in_{n+1}$). For any collection of radii $\{r_p\}_{p \in X}$ with $r_p \in (0,\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p})$, $u \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $\supp{u} \cap B_{r_p}(p)$ is finite for all $p \in X$, sequence $v_n \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$ such that $\sup_n \|v_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$ and $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v_n) \to u$, and $c \in (0,1)$, there exists another sequence $\tilde{v}_n \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $\|\tilde{v}_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$ for every $n \geq 1$, \item $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n) \to u$, \item for all $p_i \in X$ and $n \geq i$, $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i) \subseteq \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i)$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: an ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ such that $\mathcal{F}in \subseteq \mathcal{I}$ and $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective
nodes.statement_short: Iterating Lemma 6.21 over an enumeration and diagonalizing, supports can be reduced eventually in every ball.
nodes.label: lem:sequence2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.22
nodes.statement: Let $\{r_p\}_{p \in X}$, $u$, $v_n$, and $c$ be as above. Applying Lemma \ref{lem:sequence1} with $p = p_1$, $r = r_{p_1}$, $u = u$, $v_n = v_n$, and $c = c$, we get a sequence $\tilde{v}_n^1$ with $\sup_n \|\tilde{v}_n^1\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n^1) \to u$, and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n^1} \cap B_{cr_{p_{1}}}(p_{1}) = \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_{1}}}(p_{1})$. Then we apply Lemma \ref{lem:sequence1} again with $p = p_2$, $r = r_{p_2}$, $u = u$, $v_n = \tilde{v}_n^1$, and $c=c$ to get a sequence $\tilde{v}_n^2$ with $\sup_n \|\tilde{v}_n^2\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n^2) \to u$, and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n^2} \cap B_{cr_{p_{2}}}(p_{2}) = \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_{2}}}(p_{2})$ and also $\supp{\tilde{v}_n^2} \cap B_{cr_{p_{1}}}(p_{1}) \subseteq \supp{\tilde{v}_n^1} \cap B_{cr_{p_{1}}}(p_{1}) = \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_{1}}}(p_{1})$. Iterating, we get, for all $i$, sequences $\tilde{v}_n^i$ such that $\sup_n \|\tilde{v}_n^i\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n^i) \to u$, and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n^i} \cap B_{cr_{p_{i'}}}(p_{i'}) \subseteq \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_{i'}}}(p_{i'})$ for all $i' \leq i$. By diagonalizing, we can find a single sequence $\tilde{v}_n$ with the required properties.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 6.21 successively at $p_1, p_2, \dots$ and diagonalize.

nodes.name: First ball
nodes.statement: Let $\{r_p\}_{p \in X}$, $u$, $v_n$, and $c$ be as above. Applying Lemma \ref{lem:sequence1} with $p = p_1$, $r = r_{p_1}$, $u = u$, $v_n = v_n$, and $c = c$, we get a sequence $\tilde{v}_n^1$ with $\sup_n \|\tilde{v}_n^1\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n^1) \to u$, and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n^1} \cap B_{cr_{p_{1}}}(p_{1}) = \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_{1}}}(p_{1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.21 at $p_1$.

nodes.name: Second ball
nodes.statement: Then we apply Lemma \ref{lem:sequence1} again with $p = p_2$, $r = r_{p_2}$, $u = u$, $v_n = \tilde{v}_n^1$, and $c=c$ to get a sequence $\tilde{v}_n^2$ with $\sup_n \|\tilde{v}_n^2\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n^2) \to u$, and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n^2} \cap B_{cr_{p_{2}}}(p_{2}) = \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_{2}}}(p_{2})$ and also $\supp{\tilde{v}_n^2} \cap B_{cr_{p_{1}}}(p_{1}) \subseteq \supp{\tilde{v}_n^1} \cap B_{cr_{p_{1}}}(p_{1}) = \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_{1}}}(p_{1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.21 at $p_2$ preserves the first ball.

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: Iterating, we get, for all $i$, sequences $\tilde{v}_n^i$ such that $\sup_n \|\tilde{v}_n^i\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n^i) \to u$, and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n^i} \cap B_{cr_{p_{i'}}}(p_{i'}) \subseteq \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_{i'}}}(p_{i'})$ for all $i' \leq i$.
nodes.statement_short: Sequences for every i.

nodes.name: Diagonalize
nodes.statement: By diagonalizing, we can find a single sequence $\tilde{v}_n$ with the required properties.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal sequence works.

nodes.name: Restriction R^J_I is a 7-semi-embedding
nodes.statement: Assume $X$ is countable with enumeration $X = \{p_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$. Assume $X$ is discrete. Fix an ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ such that $\mathcal{F}in \subseteq \mathcal{I}$ and $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective. Set $\mathcal{J} := \ulm{\mathcal{I}}$ so that Theorem \ref{thm:injective} implies $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is also injective (for example, $\mathcal{I} = \mathcal{F}in_n$ and $\mathcal{J} = \mathcal{F}in_{n+1}$). The map $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}: \LF{\mathcal{J},X} \to \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ is a 7-semi-embedding.
assumptions: an ideal $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ such that $\mathcal{F}in \subseteq \mathcal{I}$ and $R^{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{F}in}$ is injective
nodes.statement_short: For countable discrete X, restriction from LF(ulm(I),X) to LF(I,X) is a 7-semi-embedding.
nodes.label: thm:semiembedding

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.23
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:injective}, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}$ is injective, so it remains to show \\ $\overline{R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})} \subseteq R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(7B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})$. Suppose $v'_n \in\LF{\mathcal{J},X}$ and $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v'_n) \to u' \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ with $\sup_n \|v'_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$ and $\|u'\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$. Let $c \in (0,1)$. Set $r_p := c \cdot \rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}$ for each $p \in X$. By Lemma \ref{lem:quotientfinite}, $u' = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + u$ for some $w \in \LF{X}$ and $u \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ with $\|w\| + \|u\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$ and $\supp{u} \cap B_{r_p}(p)$ is finite for each $p \in X$. Set $v_n := v'_n - R_{\mathcal{J}}(w)$ so that $\sup_n\|v_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 2$ and $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v_n) \to u$. Then we apply Lemma \ref{lem:sequence2} with $r_p = r_p$, $u = u$, $v_n = v_n$, $c = c$ to obtain a sequence $\tilde{v}_n$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\|\tilde{v}_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 2$ for all $n \geq 1$, \item $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n) \to u$, \item for all $p_i \in X$ and $n \geq i$, $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i) \subseteq \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i)$. \end{enumerate} Fix $n \geq 1$, and set $Y := X \setminus (\cup_{i \leq n} B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i))$ and $F := \cup_{i \leq n} (\supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i))$ so that $F$ is finite and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \subseteq Y \cup F$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ small enough so that $B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \subseteq X \setminus (\cup_{i \leq n} B_{c^2r_{p_i}}(p_i))$. Then Lemma \ref{lem:supp} implies \begin{equation} \tilde{v}_n \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{Z_n} \end{equation} where $Z_n := F \cup (X \setminus (\cup_{i \leq n} B_{c^2r_{p_i}}(p_i)))$. Set $\rho(p,q) := c^3\min(\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{J}}{q}) \leq c^2r_{p}$ and for each $j \geq 1$, $Z_{n,j} := B_{\rho(p_j,q)}(p_j) \cap Z_n$. When $n \geq j$, \begin{equation} Z_{n,j} = B_{\rho(p_j,q)}(p_j) \cap F \subseteq \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_j}}(p_j). \end{equation} Suppose $\tilde{v}_n = \sum_{p \in X} c_{p,n}\delta_p$ and $u = \sum_{p \in X} c_p\delta_p$, so that $c_{p,n} \to c_p$ for each $p$. Since $\|\tilde{v}_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 2$, \eqref{eq:supp} and Lemma \ref{lem:quotientclose} allow us write \begin{equation} \sum_{p \in X} c_{p,n}\delta_p = \sum_{\substack{(p,q) \in Z_n^2 \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}}b_{(p,q),n}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in Z_n} a_{p,n} \delta_p \end{equation} with $$\sum_{\substack{(p,q) \in Z_n^2 \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}}|b_{(p,q),n}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in Z_n} |a_{p,n}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p} < 6c^{-3}.$$ For the sake of notational convenience, we'll define $b_{(p,q),n} := 0$ if $(p,q) \in X^2 \setminus Z_n^2$ or $d(p,q) > \rho(p,q)$ and $a_{p,n} := 0$ if $p \in X \setminus Z_n$ so that the above equations remain true when the first terms are summed over $X^2$ and the second over $X$. Fix a nonprincipal ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $\mathbb{N}$. It is easy to see that $|b_{(p,q),n}| \leq 6c^{-3}d(p,q)^{-1}$ and $|a_{p,n}| \leq 6c^{-3}\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}^{-1}$ for all $p\neq q \in X$ and $n \geq 1$, and thus $b_{(p,q)} := \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} b_{(p,q),n}$ and $a_p := \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} a_{p,n}$ exist. For each $p \in X$, evaluating each side of \eqref{eq:c=b} at the Lipschitz function $\mathsf{1}_p$ yields $$c_{p,n} = \sum_{q \in X} (b_{(p,q),n}-b_{(q,p),n}) + a_{p,n}$$ $$=\sum_{\substack{q \in Z_n \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}} (b_{(p,q),n}-b_{(q,p),n}) + a_{p,n}.$$ Then for each $j \geq 1$, combining this with the definition of $Z_{n,j}$ gives $$c_{p_j,n} = \sum_{q \in Z_{n,j}} (b_{(p_j,q),n}-b_{(q,p_j),n}) + a_{p_j,n}.$$ By \eqref{eq:Znj}, the set over which this sum is performed, $Z_{n,j}$, is eventually (depending on $j$) contained in the fixed finite set $\supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_j}}(p_j)$. Thus we can interchange the sum and $\mathcal{U}$-limit to obtain $$c_{p_j} = \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} c_{p_j},n = \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{q \in X} (b_{(p_j,q),n}-b_{(q,p_j),n}) + a_{p_j,n}$$ $$= \sum_{q \in X} \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} (b_{(p_j,q),n}-b_{(q,p_j),n}) + \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} a_{p_j,n}$$ $$= \sum_{q \in X} (b_{(p_j,q)}-b_{(q,p_j)}) + a_{p_j}$$ and thus $$u = \sum_{p_j \in X} c_{p_j}\delta_{p_j} = \sum_{p_j \in X} \sum_{q \in X}(b_{(p_j,q)}-b_{(q,p_j)})\delta_{p_j} + a_{p_j}\delta_{p_j}$$ $$= \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in X} a_p \delta_p$$ and $$\sum_{(p,q) \in X^2} \|b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q)\|_{\mathcal{J}} + \sum_{p \in X} \|a_{p} \delta_p\|_{\mathcal{J}}$$ $$\leq \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in X} |a_{p}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}$$ $$= \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}\mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty}|b_{(p,q),n}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in X} \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty}|a_{p,n}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}$$ $$\leq \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}|b_{(p,q),n}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in X}|a_{p,n}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p} \leq 6c^{-3}$$ where the second to last inequality is Fatou's lemma. Thus, we set $v = \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in X} a_{p} \delta_p \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$, so the last two formulae give us $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v) = u$ and $\|v\|_{\mathcal{J}} \leq 6c^{-3}$. Then $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(R_{\mathcal{J}}(w)+v) = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + u = u'$ and $\|R_{\mathcal{J}}(w)+v\|_{\mathcal{J}} \leq 1 + 6c^{-3}$. Taking $c \nearrow 1$ shows $\overline{R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})} \subseteq R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(7B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Given $R(v'_n)\to u'$, finitize u (Lemma 6.18), localize supports (Lemmas 6.22, 6.20), decompose with short jumps (Lemma 6.16) and pass to an ultrafilter limit of coefficients. Eventual finiteness of the relevant supports lets the limit commute with the sums.

nodes.name: Injectivity; reduce to closure inclusion
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:injective}, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}$ is injective, so it remains to show \\ $\overline{R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})} \subseteq R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(7B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity by Theorem 6.13; remains the closure inclusion.

nodes.name: Sequences and radii
nodes.statement: Suppose $v'_n \in\LF{\mathcal{J},X}$ and $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v'_n) \to u' \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ with $\sup_n \|v'_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$ and $\|u'\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$. Let $c \in (0,1)$. Set $r_p := c \cdot \rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}$ for each $p \in X$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $v'_n \to u'$, c and $r_p$.

nodes.name: Finitize u
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:quotientfinite}, $u' = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + u$ for some $w \in \LF{X}$ and $u \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ with $\|w\| + \|u\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$ and $\supp{u} \cap B_{r_p}(p)$ is finite for each $p \in X$. Set $v_n := v'_n - R_{\mathcal{J}}(w)$ so that $\sup_n\|v_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 2$ and $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v_n) \to u$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.18 splits off w; shift $v_n$.

nodes.name: Reduce supports
nodes.statement: Then we apply Lemma \ref{lem:sequence2} with $r_p = r_p$, $u = u$, $v_n = v_n$, $c = c$ to obtain a sequence $\tilde{v}_n$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\|\tilde{v}_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 2$ for all $n \geq 1$, \item $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n) \to u$, \item
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.22 gives $\tilde v_n$.

nodes.name: Eventual support reduction
nodes.statement: for all $p_i \in X$ and $n \geq i$, $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i) \subseteq \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Supports of $\tilde v_n$ eventually lie in supp u within each ball.

nodes.name: Localize via Lemma 6.20
nodes.statement: Fix $n \geq 1$, and set $Y := X \setminus (\cup_{i \leq n} B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i))$ and $F := \cup_{i \leq n} (\supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i))$ so that $F$ is finite and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \subseteq Y \cup F$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ small enough so that $B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \subseteq X \setminus (\cup_{i \leq n} B_{c^2r_{p_i}}(p_i))$. Then Lemma \ref{lem:supp} implies \begin{equation} \tilde{v}_n \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{Z_n} \end{equation} where $Z_n := F \cup (X \setminus (\cup_{i \leq n} B_{c^2r_{p_i}}(p_i)))$.
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde v_n \in LF(J, Z_n)$.

nodes.name: Sets Z_{n,j}
nodes.statement: Set $\rho(p,q) := c^3\min(\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{J}}{q}) \leq c^2r_{p}$ and for each $j \geq 1$, $Z_{n,j} := B_{\rho(p_j,q)}(p_j) \cap Z_n$. When $n \geq j$, \begin{equation} Z_{n,j} = B_{\rho(p_j,q)}(p_j) \cap F \subseteq \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_j}}(p_j). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define $\rho$ and $Z_{n,j}$; eventually inside supp u.

nodes.name: Short-jump decomposition
nodes.statement: Suppose $\tilde{v}_n = \sum_{p \in X} c_{p,n}\delta_p$ and $u = \sum_{p \in X} c_p\delta_p$, so that $c_{p,n} \to c_p$ for each $p$. Since $\|\tilde{v}_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 2$, \eqref{eq:supp} and Lemma \ref{lem:quotientclose} allow us write \begin{equation} \sum_{p \in X} c_{p,n}\delta_p = \sum_{\substack{(p,q) \in Z_n^2 \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}}b_{(p,q),n}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in Z_n} a_{p,n} \delta_p \end{equation} with $$\sum_{\substack{(p,q) \in Z_n^2 \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}}|b_{(p,q),n}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in Z_n} |a_{p,n}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p} < 6c^{-3}.$$ For the sake of notational convenience, we'll define $b_{(p,q),n} := 0$ if $(p,q) \in X^2 \setminus Z_n^2$ or $d(p,q) > \rho(p,q)$ and $a_{p,n} := 0$ if $p \in X \setminus Z_n$ so that the above equations remain true when the first terms are summed over $X^2$ and the second over $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.16 gives coefficients b, a with weight < $6c^{-3}$.

nodes.name: Ultralimits of coefficients
nodes.statement: Fix a nonprincipal ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $\mathbb{N}$. It is easy to see that $|b_{(p,q),n}| \leq 6c^{-3}d(p,q)^{-1}$ and $|a_{p,n}| \leq 6c^{-3}\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}^{-1}$ for all $p\neq q \in X$ and $n \geq 1$, and thus $b_{(p,q)} := \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} b_{(p,q),n}$ and $a_p := \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} a_{p,n}$ exist.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients bounded, so ultralimits exist.

nodes.name: Coefficient identity
nodes.statement: For each $p \in X$, evaluating each side of \eqref{eq:c=b} at the Lipschitz function $\mathsf{1}_p$ yields $$c_{p,n} = \sum_{q \in X} (b_{(p,q),n}-b_{(q,p),n}) + a_{p,n}$$ $$=\sum_{\substack{q \in Z_n \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}} (b_{(p,q),n}-b_{(q,p),n}) + a_{p,n}.$$ Then for each $j \geq 1$, combining this with the definition of $Z_{n,j}$ gives $$c_{p_j,n} = \sum_{q \in Z_{n,j}} (b_{(p_j,q),n}-b_{(q,p_j),n}) + a_{p_j,n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate at $1_p$ to express $c_{p,n}$ through b, a.

nodes.name: Interchange limit and sum
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:Znj}, the set over which this sum is performed, $Z_{n,j}$, is eventually (depending on $j$) contained in the fixed finite set $\supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_j}}(p_j)$. Thus we can interchange the sum and $\mathcal{U}$-limit to obtain $$c_{p_j} = \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} c_{p_j},n = \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{q \in X} (b_{(p_j,q),n}-b_{(q,p_j),n}) + a_{p_j,n}$$ $$= \sum_{q \in X} \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} (b_{(p_j,q),n}-b_{(q,p_j),n}) + \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} a_{p_j,n}$$ $$= \sum_{q \in X} (b_{(p_j,q)}-b_{(q,p_j)}) + a_{p_j}$$ and thus $$u = \sum_{p_j \in X} c_{p_j}\delta_{p_j} = \sum_{p_j \in X} \sum_{q \in X}(b_{(p_j,q)}-b_{(q,p_j)})\delta_{p_j} + a_{p_j}\delta_{p_j}$$ $$= \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in X} a_p \delta_p$$ and $$\sum_{(p,q) \in X^2} \|b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q)\|_{\mathcal{J}} + \sum_{p \in X} \|a_{p} \delta_p\|_{\mathcal{J}}$$ $$\leq \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in X} |a_{p}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}$$ $$= \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}\mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty}|b_{(p,q),n}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in X} \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty}|a_{p,n}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}$$ $$\leq \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}|b_{(p,q),n}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in X}|a_{p,n}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p} \leq 6c^{-3}$$ where the second to last inequality is Fatou's lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Finite eventual supports allow interchange; Fatou bounds the norm.

nodes.name: Limit preimage
nodes.statement: Thus, we set $v = \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in X} a_{p} \delta_p \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$, so the last two formulae give us $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v) = u$ and $\|v\|_{\mathcal{J}} \leq 6c^{-3}$. Then $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(R_{\mathcal{J}}(w)+v) = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + u = u'$ and $\|R_{\mathcal{J}}(w)+v\|_{\mathcal{J}} \leq 1 + 6c^{-3}$.
nodes.statement_short: v maps to u with norm ≤ $6c^{-3}$.

nodes.name: Conclude constant 7
nodes.statement: Taking $c \nearrow 1$ shows $\overline{R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})} \subseteq R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(7B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Let c → 1.

nodes.name: Localization of tilde v_n
nodes.statement: \tilde{v}_n \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{Z_n}
nodes.label: eq:supp

nodes.name: Z_{n,j} eventually in supp u
nodes.statement: Z_{n,j} = B_{\rho(p_j,q)}(p_j) \cap F \subseteq \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_j}}(p_j).
nodes.label: eq:Znj

nodes.name: Short-jump representation of tilde v_n
nodes.statement: \sum_{p \in X} c_{p,n}\delta_p = \sum_{\substack{(p,q) \in Z_n^2 \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}}b_{(p,q),n}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in Z_n} a_{p,n} \delta_p
nodes.label: eq:c=b

nodes.name: Little Lipschitz space lip_0 and uniform point separation
nodes.statement: Recall that $\lip{X}$ is the closed subspace of $\Lip{X}$ defined by $f \in \lip{X}$ if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $0<d(x,y)<\delta$ implies $|f(y)-f(x)| \leq \varepsilon d(x,y)$. Whenever $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ is an ideal, we define $\boldsymbol{\lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}} := \lip{X} \cap \Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$. We say that $\lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ \emph{separates points uniformly} if there exists $a < \infty$ such that for every $F \subseteq X$ finite and $g \in B_{\Lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}}$, there exists $f \in \lip{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ such that $\|f\| \leq a$ and $f$ and $g$ agree on $F$.

nodes.name: Weaver's predual theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{K} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ denote the ideal of compact subsets. If $\lip{\mathcal{K}}{X}$ separates points uniformly, then $\LF{\mathcal{K}}{X} = \lip{\mathcal{K}}{X}^*$.
assumptions: $\mathcal{K} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ denote the ideal of compact subsets
nodes.label: thm:predual

nodes.name: Extension of Weaver's theorem to locally compact spaces
nodes.statement: The theorem is stated there for compact metric spaces, but the proof easily extends to compactly supported Lipschitz functions on a locally compact metric space.

nodes.name: LF(Fin,X) is a dual space for discrete X
nodes.statement: If $X$ is discrete, then $\LF{\mathcal{F}in}{X} = \Lip{\mathcal{F}in}{X}^*$.
nodes.label: cor:predual

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 6.26
nodes.statement: Assume $X$ is discrete. Then $\mathcal{K} = \mathcal{F}in$ and \\ $\lip{\mathcal{K}}{X} = \lip{\mathcal{F}in}{X} = \Lip{\mathcal{F}in}{X}$. The corollary then follows from Theorem \ref{thm:predual}.
nodes.statement_short: For discrete X, compact = finite and lip = Lip on finitely supported functions; apply Weaver's theorem.

nodes.name: Equivalence of RNP and Schur for Lipschitz free spaces
nodes.statement: Are the Radon-Nikod\'ym and Schur properties equivalent for Lipschitz free spaces?

nodes.name: Failure of RNP and L^1 isomorphs
nodes.statement: Does a Lipschitz free space failing to have RNP necessarily contain an isomorph of $L^1(\mathbb{R})$?

nodes.name: Failure of RNP and positive measure subsets of R
nodes.statement: Does $\LF{X}$ failing to have the RNP imply $X$ contains a biLipschitz copy of a compact, positive measure subset of $\mathbb{R}$?

nodes.name: L^1 isomorphs and positive measure subsets of R
nodes.statement: Does $\LF{X}$ containing an isomorph of $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ imply $X$ contains a biLipschitz copy of a compact, positive measure subset of $\mathbb{R}$?

nodes.name: Converses of Questions 7.2-7.4 hold
nodes.statement: The converse to each of the last three questions has a positive answer.
conclusions: The converse to each of the last three questions has a positive answer

nodes.name: Proof of the converses
nodes.statement: This is because $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ fails to have the RNP and $\LF{X}$ is isomorphic to $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ whenever $X$ is biLipschitz equivalent to a compact, positive measure subset of $\mathbb{R}$ (\cite[Corollary 3.4]{Godard}).
nodes.statement_short: $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ fails RNP and LF of a positive-measure compact subset of R is isomorphic to $L^1$ (Godard).
